thus it says, "establishing one's own habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*). Answer: Regarding the terms "seed" and "cultivation," the word "seed" encompasses both those newly perfumed and acquired, whereas "cultivation" is spoken of only in reference to what is newly acquired.
However, there are many difficulties [with this view], which will be carefully analyzed later.

Section. Regarding the phrase "attaining by taking a superior object as a condition" and so forth: this clarifies that what is attained through causes such as hearing the superior [teachings] and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) below is the cultivation of what has already been attained;
one does not cultivate what has not yet been attained.

Section. One who cultivates a lower stage to reach a higher one must necessarily have previously attained that higher state. If one has never previously attained that higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the lower stage lacks the power to cultivate the higher.
If one has previously attained it but subsequently lost it, the lower stage can again cause the seeds of the higher state to be newly perfumed and increased.
Otherwise, why specify "previously attained"? Alternatively, there may also be an increase of both the original and the newly perfumed types.

Therefore, it is said that [the concentration] has never been attained before. If this is necessarily so, it is because through repeated cultivation with the desire to enter a higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one causes the seeds of that higher stage—the primary causes—to increase in each moment of mind. In the second moment, one then gives rise to that absorption. Otherwise, [it would not be possible].
On what basis can that meditative concentration of a higher stage arise? It is not because of a completely remote mind.
As for the beginner: one who has attained only the first dhyāna but has not yet attained the other stages.

Regarding the passage concerning those who practice in gradual proximity and those who explain it: for example, a person in the form realm first cultivates the first dhyāna, and subsequently [cultivates] the desire realm.
The answer is that this is because they cultivate hearing, reflection, and so forth; thus, they cultivate two types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the lower realm.

As for the statement that the first dhyāna "only attains the cultivation of the factors" (*dharmabhāvanā*) and does not "cultivate" [other things], this is said with respect to those practicing in gradual proximity. Therefore, from the second dhyāna upward, it is as follows...
"Not cultivated" means that it has never previously been the object of intentional reflection.
Regarding "gradually approaching," this refers to cases such as when the first dhyāna gradually approaches the second dhyāna and so forth.
Regarding "because the fruit has not yet arisen," this refers to not having attained the actualized fruit of meditative concentration belonging to those higher fundamental stages.

Section. Regarding those from the eighth stage upward who are capable of contemplation up to the two natures: although their eyes and other faculties in those stages are contaminated (*sāsrava*), since this section clarifies that which is capable of contemplation and those [faculties] are not capable of contemplation, they are not excluded.

Section. If one has already eliminated [the appearances] up to the point where they are merely the aspect of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), then the contemplation involving aspects prior to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) arises in a manner similar to the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*);
this is called "homogeneous" (*jāti*). This aspect does not arise, and thus its non-attainment constitutes the attainment of abandonment.
Alternatively, it is seen that the *vijñaptimātratā* contemplation practiced prior to the Path of Seeing constitutes the true lineage (*gotra*).

Regarding the phrase "for a long time and for the most part," this refers to the four stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), wherein one contemplates the two natures throughout these four positions.

The period is called "long. Even during the brief moments of *kṣānti* (patience) and the *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas), there is also realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

therefore, these two natures are designated as "majority" (*bāhulika*). The commentary states: "Brief time and a small portion": the *laukikāgradharma* stage is termed "brief time," and the stage of *kṣānti* is termed "small portion."
Section. Regarding the statement that "through *vipaśyanā* one attains this state": Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) take birth according to their karma;

because they possess karma pertaining to the three realms, they are able to be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). If one were not a bodhisattva, who in that realm could, with a single mind, take all phenomena as an object?
Therefore, it is known that in all three realms one can give rise to this contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā-vipaśyanā*). This is based on the latter [category].
Regarding the statement, "From the eighth stage upward until the attainment of Bodhi," this is spoken according to the definitive teaching.

Because from the seventh stage downward, one undergoes *pariṇāmiki-jāti* (transformation-rebirth) without certainty, it is said that [the stages] pervade the three realms; this can be understood by reflection.

Section: Regarding the phrase "those who have not yet undergone birth" up to "arising based on a physical body": because those who have not yet undergone birth do not fear birth and death, they pertain to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Their arising based on a body occurs prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). Because Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*) undergo transformation-birth (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*) and have not yet reached certainty, they may rely upon both realms.
Therefore, this now includes them collectively; it does not refer solely to those of gradual enlightenment (*jianwu*). Furthermore, the commentary explains the "seventh stage."

Previously, according to the theory of gradual enlightenment, it was held that one does not undergo rebirth; yet, what prevents those who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle from reaching the seventh stage and no longer undergoing transformation?
If this were not the case, since the matter of sudden enlightenment has already been clarified previously, why would it need to be stated again now?

Section: Regarding "because of the mastery of compassionate vows in taking birth according to circumstances," this explains that those who have attained the two fruits differ from Bodhisattvas who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) in their manner of taking birth.
Section: Regarding "nor is it because of cultivation that rebirth is permitted," prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), Bodhisattvas take birth in accordance with their karma.

[They] are able to be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Now, they differ from those [others] in that they are not born in the formless realm; this is because their cultivation is spontaneous (*anābhoga*).

The section states: "Those who have already attained the untainted (*anāsrava*)" refers to persons who have attained the first three fruits. "Because the power of their karma is great" explains the Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Or perhaps it is permitted because [the practitioner] gives rise to a state of weariness toward the defilements of the lower realms. The intent of this explanation is as follows:

Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) possess afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the three realms, yet they are able to be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); the same applies to those who have attained the two fruits [of the śrāvaka path]. Why, then, could [the bodhisattva] not be born there?

If that were so, since one relies upon a superior physical basis (*āśraya*) to realize *bodhi*, how could one attain the great *bodhi* of a Buddha after having been born in the formless realm? Is this the case?
This is difficult. Therefore, it is now stated: "It is not because one born above feels revulsion for the defilements below.

This means that it is not the case that those born in the formless realms (ārūpya) have severed [birth] by feeling revulsion for the defilements below and thus do not take birth there; rather, for this reason, they are reborn in the fourth dhyāna.
Although this principle exists, it does not equal the previous explanation.

Section. Regarding those who have undergone rebirth, up to the point of generating the resolve for awakening and thereafter: these individuals who have undergone rebirth, because they fear birth and death, first attain and subsequently attain [the fruit] within the desire realm.

Section. Regarding those who have undergone rebirth (*saṃsaraṇa*) or those who have attained the fourth fruit and so forth: this statement that they "have undergone rebirth" does not mean they have already attained [the fruit] and can subsequently undergo rebirth in the form realm;
rather, because they have not yet attained it, they undergo rebirth first.
Regarding the passage stating that the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts say [this is] because there is not yet profound revulsion: the intended meaning of this is as follows.

When those of the three vehicles enter their own respective clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), they do so solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because among humans it is only there that the power of wisdom and understanding is most intense and sharp, thereby enabling them to sever the grasping at birth.

If it is one who attains realization gradually (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*), they may also attain it in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). If that is so, when those in the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) in the form realm turn their minds toward awakening, they will not descend again to be born below;

how could it be that they do not practice the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? Question: Regarding the attainment of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the holy teachings state only that these are first attained in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Since you allow that they may be first attained in the higher realms, the same should apply to the absorption of cessation. How does the Dharma Master explain this?
It is said: "The Form Realm is also initially attained. Regarding the phrase "initially attained in the Form Realm," this refers back to what is individually manifested.

If one turns the mind [toward enlightenment] while in the Form Realm, it is likewise considered "initially attained" in the Form Realm. If a person such as a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) cannot personally attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in the Form Realm, it is said that they will not attain it even when reborn in the Form Realm.
However, if they turn their minds [toward enlightenment], they shall immediately attain that Mahāyāna cessation.

Regarding *nirodha-samāpatti*: some say that those who have attained the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) and are reborn in the higher realms must have already attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, this attainment initially exists only in the desire realm, unlike the direct realizations (*abhisamaya*). This is also not correct.
Do those Non-returners and others necessarily attain all nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*)?

Section. Regarding those in the form realm who lack wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*): because they enter meditative absorption with only slight withdrawal of the mind, it is said that "they possess reflection.
Because they possess the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*), it is said that "they obtain hearing."
Section: Regarding "there is no form and no one who hears," the volition of the formless is the same as that of the formed; because there are no sense faculties in the formless, there is no hearing.

Section: Regarding "whether in meditative absorption or in birth," one who has attained that absorption but has not yet been born there is called "one in absorption," while one who has been born there is called "one in birth."

Section. Regarding the comprehension of the phenomena of the three realms by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): Question: Since a mind of the formless realm perceives sounds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), this is not the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Why, then, can it be said that there is no hearing in the formless realm? Answer: That [wisdom] arises solely from a mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and hears the Dharma and so forth;

furthermore, because it is without signs (*animitta*), it is not termed "hearing. Question: From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, that [mind] is exclusively in a state of meditative concentration. What is its distinction?

Regarding the question of why this [distinction] does not apply to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), the answer is as follows: Based on the meaning, one may distinguish that there is "hearing" (*śruta*); however, since the preceding discussion was based on ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it stated that there is none.

Alternatively, it is not obtained; yet, from the perspective of conventional meaning, one may say there is hearing. A Bodhisattva of the eighth stage relies solely upon the form of the *dhātu*; since an ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*) can exist there, one may conventionally say it exists.
In the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), no such faculties exist, so it cannot be analogized. One may freely choose between these two interpretations according to one’s inclination. (From the *Chang*).
Regarding the statement "rootless" (amūlaka): it is called rootless because it is said that there is no hearing [of the Dharma].

Regarding the nine [stages] for severing afflictions: this excludes the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra). Regarding the ten [stages] for the practice of contemplation (vihāra): there are six in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and four in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), as both possess the practice of contemplation.
Section. Regarding those who say "the first five stages" refers to those common to the first five stages: [this concerns] independent greed and so forth. Question:

Since this "harming companion" (*sahāya-hiṃsaka*) latent tendency (*anuśaya*) has already been abandoned by the fifth stage, why does the Sūtra state that "among the first five stages, that which is not co-nascent is called 'harming the companion,'" and that "by the fifth stage, the companion has already been harmed"? It should rather be said that it is "among the first four stages" that which is not co-nascent.
This is called "harming the companion. In response: within the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three types of mind—entry, abiding, and emergence.

When it is said here that "harming the companion" is excluded in the five stages, this is stated with reference to the minds of abiding and emergence. Thus, one should reflect upon how it is possible for the five stages to involve harming the companion.

Section: Regarding "from subtle manifestation to non-manifestation," this refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that stage; they are distinguished as active or inactive based on whether they have been suppressed or not. Section:

Regarding "in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, once innate [self-view] has been severed, afflictions do not arise," this means that because one has already severed the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) at the outset in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, craving [no longer arises].
"Equal non-arising," excluding the secret designation of "the four," refers precisely to the *Ākāśagarbha-samādhi*. Having attained this samādhi, one encompasses ten thousand virtues;
it is like desiring to contain and store all things within empty space.
Section: Regarding the ultimate abandonment of the two types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). This refers to the two latent dispositions that are weakened by the destruction of their companions.

Section: Regarding the attainment of faith and non-retrogression at the sixth mind-moment. Question: As for the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), they are capable of generating [the path] such that it is difficult to be overcome.
Since you speak of "non-retrogression," by what power is this established specifically during the stage of applied practice (*prayoga*)? Answer: At this stage, one does not slander cause and effect.
These are called the non-retrogression of faith; yet their power is still weak and inferior, so they do not receive the name of "following power.

As explained extensively in the *Fahua chao*, in the chapter on the distinction between the coarse, uncommon view of self and [the other], both are termed "coarse. By subduing these two, one is said to have "exited the triple world."

This should be understood according to the verse. The meaning of the text explains that this fourth stage (*vihāra*) is characterized by the non-attachment to phenomena; thus, one knows that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is suppressed.

Because it is suppressed, one is able to transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*). As for the temporary suppression and removal of these two seeds, it is because both the *tīrthikas* and the heterodox practitioners are attached to a self.

Section. Third, regarding the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): this refers to the obscuration consisting in the fear of suffering held by Śrāvakas. Both this and the mind of equanimity of Pratyekabuddhas constitute cognitive obscurations. Section. Regarding the "mind of equanimity" of Pratyekabuddhas:

it is the relinquishing of that mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*) to enter into quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). Because it obstructs the transformation of others, it is thus [an obscuration]. One attains...

Regarding the name "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*): it is used here with the term "long-term suffering" (*dīrgha-duḥkha*) to distinguish it from that of the śrāvakas, and thus a distinct designation is established.

As for the statement in the chapter that "the first two afflictions (*kleśa*) persist until their severance by the diamond-like [samādhi]," this is spoken in reference to the afflictions based upon which [the obstruction exists].

Section. Regarding the statement that the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) necessarily entails the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*): Question: Since phenomena necessarily entail persons, how can it be that there are three minds for the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), yet only two [minds] are attained?
This is because the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena exists separately. Answer: From the perspective of seeing reality, there are only two;
however, according to the preparatory practices (*prayoga*)—such as those concerning Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*)—three are established. Thus, they are made into three types.

Section: Regarding the "Discrimination of the 'Conforming to the Previous Clause' in the Contemplation of Consciousness-Only": Consciousness-only is necessarily the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), but the emptiness of persons is not necessarily consciousness-only.
Therefore, it may conform to what precedes, but it cannot conform to what follows.

Section: Regarding the statement that "the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is likewise in relation to consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*)," it is as follows: the emptiness of phenomena necessarily entails consciousness-only, but consciousness-only does not necessarily entail the emptiness of phenomena.

This refers to the consciousness-only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). This is known through the principles of this section. To speak according to the subsequent parts of this passage, one must examine each line of the text individually before making such a claim.
It is a false assertion to state it otherwise.
Regarding the various chapters on the vehicles (*yāna*): as for the *Mahāyāna*, *mahā* means "great" and *yāna* is called "vehicle.

Thus, one should know that the Mahāyāna which accords with and leads to the ultimate teaching consists of the expressive teachings—whether they be the fundamental teachings or the provisional teachings.
Both of these are called "conforming to the Mahāyāna. The term "conforming" (*anuloma*) refers to the practice and so forth. Furthermore, based on this, one should know that [the text] says:

"The nine knowledges up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*")—namely, the two knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are termed "general," while each of the four truths is termed "specific.

Together with the former, there are six. Regarding the knowledges of the four truths, when they are categorized as "confused," they are simply the knowledges of phenomena and subsequent knowledge; thus, the general terms are used to indicate them.

Regarding the two knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), there is no further differentiation among the four truths. Together with the conventional, exhaustion, and non-arising knowledges, these constitute nine.
Question: Why is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) excluded from the ten? Answer: Briefly, there are two explanations. First, because it is not a definitive realization (*pramāṇa*).

Of the two [categories], eight knowledges are untainted (*anāsrava*), while conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is tainted (*sāsrava*). Only the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) permeates both the tainted and the untainted.

Since there is nothing outside these nine, they are not mentioned further. This has been verified by examining the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (both upper and lower sections) as well as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Section. If it is argued that the so-called "indeterminate nature" (aniyata-gotra) is not a cause because it is subject to regression, we reply:

it is taught that those of indeterminate nature who have previously practiced may abandon the Great [Vehicle] and regress to seek the Small. Furthermore, the great practices they have cultivated are not the skillful means for the fruits of that Small [Vehicle].

Section One: Those who have previously attained the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). This refers to those who have previously attained the stages conducive to penetration of a Śrāvaka.
Section Two: Those who have previously attained the attainment of realization. This refers to those who have already attained the fruits of a Śrāvaka.

Section Three: Regarding those who have not previously attained but now attain realization—namely, those who have not yet attained *nirvedha* (penetrating insight) and its fruit, the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddhas*)—because the duration of their initial refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) is long, they become those with dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*).
As for those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*) who refine their faculties prior to that, because the duration is short, they remain as such.

Furthermore, regarding those who have attained *nirvedha-bhāvanā* and reach the fruit without further refining their faculties: [it is asked] do they also refine their faculties? [The answer is: they do.

Regarding the eighth minor section of the *Yandeng* (Lamp for Examining the Meaning), the second intention states: "The śrāvakas and others in the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra were of indeterminate nature."
Chapter. Furthermore, there are minor portions that rely upon sound; this refers to awakening to the Way by taking the sounds of wind, trees, water, and so forth as conditions.
Alternatively, it is said that when one is about to reach the fruit, one also seeks out and contemplates those teachings from afar to give rise to realization.

Section: Regarding those whose destiny as humans or devas is shallow and proximate, rather than ultimate—these individuals of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) are unable to transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*), and thus are termed "non-ultimate.
It does not mean that these individuals could become noble ones (*ārya*) and instead remain among humans or devas; rather, they are termed non-ultimate for this reason.

Alternatively, it may be that those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) are not separately clarified here because their destiny is ultimately [liberated]; they simply abide wherever they happen to be.
Because it is subsumed within the [specific] realms (*dhātu*), the former interpretation should be accepted as correct.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that "the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) taught in the sūtras and śāstras is actually indeterminate": it is said to be indeterminate because those who enter directly are designated as the "One Vehicle," whereas those who enter by way of a circuitous route are designated as the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*).
Section. Regarding the phrase "the biased views of the Hīnayāna after the cessation [of the Buddha]," it is asked:
If, during the Buddha’s lifetime, various followers of the Hīnayāna all claimed that the palace was his final birth and clung to the six-foot body as the true Buddha;

and furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* and other texts, the Buddha attained enlightenment in thirty-four moments while still dwelling in the world—does this not mean that such attachments existed while the Buddha was present?

How can it be said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Hīnayāna represents a distorted view? Furthermore, the Buddha himself stated: "Having abandoned impermanent form, one attains permanent form;
the same applies to the remaining aggregates. If one were to say that those who cling to this particular perspective have refuted the Mahāyāna, what fault would there be in that?
Answer: Their original intention was that those who formerly studied the Mahāyāna clung to it as being ultimate. To refute them now is what is meant by [refuting the Mahāyāna].
This refutes three [points]. At present, while the Buddha is in the world, there are no followers of the Mahāyāna who cling to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as being ultimate.
In reality, even within the Hīnayāna, one clings to the *nirmāṇakāya* as being ultimate; however, [the scriptures] extensively establish various distinctions.

Now, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this is discussed based on the prevalent discourse (*adhikāra*). There is no fault in this general application. One should examine the *Jñānaprasthāna*, the *Āgamas*, and other sūtras, where it is clearly stated that there are thirty [types of Arhats].

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the three wheels, and the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*): as for the fact that various editions refer to "four" while others say "three," one should consult the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.

Regarding the chapter on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the "meeting of cause and fruit" refers to what is taught in the Mahāyāna concerning the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); this is the meeting of practice. [The text concludes with] the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
Regarding "not ultimate," this refers to the chapter on "Realizing the Fruit.
As for the statement that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also speaks of the One Vehicle— since it states that buddha-nature constitutes the One Vehicle and so forth—
this will be examined later.

Regarding the passage, "In every chapter of the various treasuries, has the Buddha-sun set?": Question: It is said in the Western Regions and elsewhere that when Kāśyapa ascended the mountain and struck the gong, the sound reached throughout the trichiliocosm and was known by the noble Kauṇḍinya.
Why, then, is it asked now whether the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa? Answer: For the time being, there are two explanations.
Regarding the question of knowing for oneself within a single lifetime: there is no need to reconcile the differing explanations of the two schools.
As for "great beings who have passed away," both the Buddha and Śāriputra are called great beings; thus, there is no contradiction.
Chapter. "I have lost my Great Master who has transcended desire. The Great Master who has transcended desire is the Buddha.
"My Upādhyāya has also passed away" refers to Śāriputra. Thus, I have now lost these two Great Masters.
Chapter: On the Extinction of Fetters and the Exhaustion of Outflows. He reflected to himself that although he had served the Buddha for a long time, today he was suddenly led away.
Thereupon, moved by grief and resentment, his various outflows were completely exhausted.
"Chapter. "That which resembles the summit of a mountain" refers to the summit of Mount Sumeru. "Chapter.
"The Unextinguished One" refers to Aniruddha. Because he caused lamps to be lit so that they would not be extinguished, he was named after this cause.
Section. Regarding the statement "the lamp of wisdom for ignorance": wisdom is the lamp for that ignorance; this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
Section. Regarding "the celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, and so forth": these celestial Māras and others, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, also speak of their past causes.

Chapter: Inquiry into the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and Their Respective Differences. This chapter consists of a question and answer regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Because it illuminates the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of each of these twelve links individually, it is called "Entering into Their Respective Differences" (*pratyeka-bheda-praveśa*). Alternatively, it is said that "entering into each" refers to entering the Three Piṭakas (*tripiṭaka*), hence the name "Entering into Differences.
However, this is likely not the case; for how would "entering into each" differ from the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (*kṣudraka-piṭaka*)? One should consult that tradition.

Section. These three are all abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). To abandon these refers precisely to doubt (*vicikitsā*), the two types of extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Attachment to suffering and pleasure is termed the "two extremes."

Section: Those who fear the desire realm are those who cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by means of the desire realm. Those who fear the three realms attain liberation from the three realms through wisdom (*prajñā*).

Section: The meaning of "holding" (*piṭaka*) is the meaning of "repository" (*kośa*). This first explains the sense of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*); this explanation [further] clarifies the dual gathering of the meanings expressed (*vācya*).
And because both [the object] and the expressive dharma are designated as "knowledge," it is so called.

Regarding the *dharmapada* (chapter/verse), the term "contradictory compound" (*dvandva*)—the intent of this explanation is that it is not the case that two distinct things are combined and thus called a "contradictory compound.
The name "Bodhisattva" is not the same as the name "sentient being" given to those who practice such conduct; they are not contradictory.

Reflect on this. Regarding the statement in the *Eleven-Faced Sūtra* that [the term] is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound: this refers to the fact that the names of Bodhisattvas differ.

For those sentient beings who practice such conduct, the general term "Bodhisattva" possesses these two contradictory meanings—namely, the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) senses. Therefore, I shall clarify this here.
Section. Regarding "the aggregates formed by the collection of views": "aggregates" (*dhātu*) means causes; it refers to the causes formed by the collection [of factors] such as those views.
Section. Regarding "because of committing an offense": this refers to the arising of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions through an unwholesome mind.
Regarding "purification": this refers to confession. Regarding "emergence": this refers to being cleared of the offense by relying on the aforementioned assembly.
Some say that the "support for renunciation" refers to the *mātṛkā*.
Regarding the term *mātṛkā*, it consists of the two syllables *a* and *i*. In the West, these are said to be the primary phonemes (*akṣara*). Now, within Buddhism, there are two kinds of *mātṛkā*:
first, the *mātṛkā* of the teachings, which refers to the Buddhist sūtras; second, the *mātṛkā* of meaning, which refers to the Abhidharma-piṭaka.

All meanings are sought by relying on this scripture; however, because [the scripture] is the source for the remaining [topics], it is explained as the meaning within the eleven divisions of the *abhidharma* (treatises). As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The Buddha's teaching is called the 'mother of instruction' (*śāsana-mātṛkā*); the treatises are called the 'mother of meaning' (*artha-mātṛkā*). Here, we take up the mother of meaning.
Chapter. Regarding the statement that "removing doubt" refers to the *sūtra* (Sūtrapiṭaka): the Piṭaka explains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Doubt is a primary obstacle to concentration;

among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), restlessness (*auddhatya*) and scattering (*vikṣepa*) are also primary obstacles to concentration. It is specifically mentioned as a secondary affliction here.

Section. Regarding "briefly there are nine conditions": within each of the Three Piṭakas, there are three conditions; these combine to form nine. It does not mean that a single Piṭaka constitutes nine.
Section. Regarding "collecting and subsuming them therein": this is because Kātyāyana compiled the teachings spoken within the Buddha’s sūtras; therefore, it...
The *Śāstrasaṃgraha* was composed by Kātyāyana. Some say it was spoken by the Buddhas through Kātyāyana; thus, the two interpretations are not fixed.
Presenting the views of these three masters: [the first] states that Kātyāyana composed that treatise, rather than compiling the Buddha’s teachings.

Chapter. How is it that the *Sūtra-piṭaka* explains the precepts up to the point where it explains the arising of both precept and concentration? It is because the *Vinaya-piṭaka* is able to produce the explanation of both precept and concentration;
furthermore, the precepts also give rise to concentration.
Chapter: On the Distinction of Attaining the Precepts. The distinction lies in attaining the Bodhisattva precepts while not attaining those of the Śrāvaka; this is what is meant by "distinction.

Regarding the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*), as for the general category, it subsumes all twelve sections because the remaining eleven are all included within the Sūtras (*sūtra*). Therefore, they are collectively categorized as ten.
Second, as for the chapters (*pariccheda*): if there were only a single verse-line and it were difficult to distinguish [the prose], there would occasionally be two lines;

although this does not constitute a full stanza, it is easy and simple to distinguish from the prose (*gadya*). If they were identical, there would be confusion; therefore, the term "chapter" is specified for clarity.
Section: Regarding those who employ the "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) response, although they do speak, it does not answer the specific matter asked; therefore, it is called a "non-response. Section:
As for the claim that both [fragrance and words] are absent in the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, I shall now offer an alternative explanation: both are present.

Since you already grant that names, phrases, and syllables are established based on fragrance, why would it be unreasonable for questions and answers to likewise depend upon fragrance? If this is not granted, then [the existence of fragrance]— (Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment, and the final clause remains incomplete.)

[The passage] "Having accumulated [merit], one should not preach the Dharma in Buddha-fields" refers to the chapter. Regarding "the mother of Kālaka": she is the mother of Viśākhā, who is designated by the name of her son.
Regarding "the Sūtra on Realms": this is the collective title for the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* and other such texts; it is established as a general designation based on common usage.

Regarding the name and title: "Dhātu" (界) has the meaning of "cause. Just as that nectar can moisten those who suffer from thirst for the Dharma, it is similar to a mirror in its ability to reflect all things.

It distinguishes between the two kinds of emptiness regarding produced phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). As noted in the *Fa-hua chao* (Excerpts on the Lotus Sūtra), no explicit textual authority from the sacred teachings has yet been seen [to support this].
"Chapter. Regarding "the one who correctly establishes the principle of the two emptinesses": this refers to Fang (方). Regarding "the one whose wisdom encompasses blessings":

this refers to Guang (廣). "Chapter. Regarding "that which should be repeated": since the prose (*gadya*) has not yet reached its conclusion, it should be repeated; the verse (*śloka*) derives its name from being based upon that [prose] repetition.
This is because the verse is not something that ought to be further versified.

Regarding the statement that "those not subsumed under other categories are called specific characteristics (betsō)," this refers specifically to the specific characteristics of marvelous phenomena (kṣudraka-dharma).

In reality, since the various remaining characteristics do not mutually subsume one another, each one could individually serve as a specific characteristic distinct from the others; however, for the time being, marvelous phenomena are cited as an example.
Section. Regarding the statement that there are twelve practices in the general exposition of the three cycles: this is cited as proof because their number is identical.

Section. As for the phrase "this is based on the existence of extensive teachings for the Śrāvakas," to say that the extensive is superior to the concise means that the Vaipulya is elucidated according to the Śrāvaka perspective.
If, however, it is based on the Bodhisattva perspective, then that which is extremely lofty and great is termed Vaipulya.
Section. Regarding "the aspiration for the Dharma up to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka alone": the aspiration for the Dharma refers to the ancillary teachings of that Vaipulya;

all should be understood according to this principle. Section. Regarding "by means of the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas... briefly distinguished from others": previously, within the six pairs and twelve [categories], it was merely...
I have briefly compared this with the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra to provide a concise summary.

Regarding the previous passage up to the *Vinaya*, the preceding text concerning the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other works was explained from one particular perspective among the six points of comparison.
It is taught that the *pratītyasamutpāda* and so forth are not included within the *sūtra-piṭaka* of the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas; this can be fully understood from the long section on the *vinaya*.
As for the statement that the *abhidharma* reaches all meanings, it is called "Abhidharma" because it investigates and analyzes the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
therefore, it pervades all twelve.
Section. This explains how the specific [terms] flow forth from the general. This specifically interprets the twelve distinct names of *Nirvāṇa*, while terms such as *Sūtra* represent the general.
From the beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), the reason for explaining the general is provided.

Section. Furthermore, regarding that which flows forth from the general [teachings] back into the general: this refers to the Vaipulya (Extensive) division. It is called "general" because it possesses two meanings:
first, it contains the ten aspects of the Mahāyāna; second, it reveals the ten aspects of the Hīnayāna. Thus, the general name "extensive" (*vaipulya*) encompasses all twelve divisions.
Within the twelve divisions, those teachings, principles, and locations that are extensive are all termed Vaipulya; therefore, the designation "Vaipulya" applies throughout all twelve.
I adopt the former explanation.
As for the passage stating, "Furthermore, there is an explanation regarding the mutual emergence [of teachings]," this interpretation is also sound from the perspective of principle.
Regarding the passage stating, "The principle is not incorrect; [it concerns] the names of the ninefold teaching," this explains the reason for the sequential order of the nine divisions.
Chapter: Regarding the fact that the principles are perfectly established and the teachings and practices are vast and extensive, this explains the reason for the latter three [chapters].
*Duanzhang* (Chapter on the Severing of Obstructions), end of Volume Two. Chapter:

Regarding "doubt concerning views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṅkṣā*) and doubt concerning the bases of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna-kāṅkṣā-sthāna*)," "doubt concerning views" refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*). "Bases" has the sense of cause (*hetu*). "Views" [refers to the underlying dispositions].

The seed of doubt is like the principle of "the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*) among the ten powers (*daśabala*); this is the meaning of the underlying reason (*yukti*). "Reason" (*so-i*) is precisely the cause (*hetu*).

Chapter: Since *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the extinction of the body, wisdom, and so forth is called the attainment of "without remainder. Without remainder.
Since it is named "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is clearly known to be the fruit of karma, for it is that which is to be abandoned.

Thus, the treatise states: "It should be known that the two obstacles consist of grasping and afflictions. Regarding "grasping," it encompasses both the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena.

Section. Regarding those who proceed toward the ultimate fruit and reach the stage beyond preparatory wisdom (*anābhisaṃskāra-jñāna*): this refers to one who, after attaining the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), seeks the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Such a person may employ the six modes of practice as preparatory application (*prayoga*) to suppress the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

The reason for this is that by gradually abandoning the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the three realms, they come to possess the sense of aspiring for the higher and loathing the lower. If, however, one has attained the first fruit but does not proceed toward no-more-learning...

One attains the six modes of practice (*ṣaḍākāra*) and thereby subdues the afflictions. The reason for this is that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) suddenly severs the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the three realms;

since there is no stage higher than the single level of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one has nothing further to aspire toward. Therefore, these six modes of practice do not constitute preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for the purpose of subduing the afflictions [of the path of seeing].

Consequently, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) possesses these six modes of practice, which are subsumed under the preparatory effort within the four paths. This concludes the discussion of the path of seeing.

Previously, the six modes of practice were not employed as preparatory application because wisdom was free from longing and aversion. In reality, when cultivating the path to transcend the two intermediate fruits, one also obtains the six modes of practice as preparatory application-wisdom;
however, the statement that they are "without training" (aśaikṣa) is made in reference to the ultimate fruit. Question:

Since a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) has only severed the six grades of afflictions in the desire realm and has not yet eliminated the higher afflictions, and since longing and aversion are absent, how can the six modes of practice serve as preparatory application?

[He] practices. [The Master] answers: It is simply that the superior grade constitutes the six practices; it is not necessary to have already attained the abandonment of the afflictions of the higher realms before they are termed "delight" and "aversion.

Therefore, the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) takes these six practices as the preparatory application (*prayoga*). Question: Regarding the skipping of the two intermediate fruits to attain the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
If the afflictions of the three realms are abandoned all at once and simultaneously, how can there be the six stages of practice (*ṣaḍ-abhisamaya*) for realizing the fruit of Arhatship?

Answer: This person who transcends the fruits does not suppress the afflictions of the three realms through the six stages; rather, they lack any superior aspiration or desire for even a single stage, namely the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

However, it is based on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that one can subdue the afflictions through the six practices and attain the ultimate; this does not mean that [this applies] to all [paths]. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Because of prior practice," etc., it has been explained extensively at the beginning of the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and thus it is not recorded here.

Section. Regarding those who rely solely on the final mental state at the end of the fourth [dhyāna]: this is precisely the school that maintains the existence of mental factors (*caitta*). The first moment is called consciousness (*vijñāna*);

the second is called feeling (*vedanā*); the third is called perception (*saṃjñā*); and the fourth is called formations (*saṃskāra*). Although these are in fact the meaning of a single mind, they are divided into four formations because they are volitional activities (*abhisamskāra*).
Since they pervade the three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*), they are termed the "path of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-mārga*).

Section: Regarding the statement "because of dull faculties, they arise individually," this means that due to dull faculties, one is unable to combine these paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and so forth into three paths;

therefore, the four paths arise separately. Some say that it is only through the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that one can sever the afflictions and give rise to the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*); since [the others] cannot sever [afflictions] and cannot [function as] the path, they are combined into one.
The distinction between the modes of activity of the three paths is as follows: this interpretation is incorrect. It speaks of the four paths arising separately for those of dull faculties;
it does not say they arise in combination. One should consult the tenth [chapter] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* for further clarification.

Section. Regarding the point that "both may be pervasive": this refers to the pervasive nature of the outflows (*āsrava*) and their suppression, as well as the fact that both karma and its fruit are severed along with their underlying substance when they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Section. There is an interpretation stating that the three types of wisdom—of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—only sever [the afflictions] upon reaching the stage of detachment (*vairāgya*).

The intention of this master is to say that all three—hearing, reflection, and cultivation—constitute preparatory application (*prayoga*). Hearing and reflection are distant and cannot suppress [the afflictions]; cultivation is the proximate preparatory application, and therefore it is able to suppress the delusions. (7)

Among the modes of attention (*manasikāra*), the two—comprehending characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) and resolute belief (*adhimokṣika*)—belong to wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*). The one type, distancing (*vairāgya*), belongs to wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).

Since the Abhidharma states that comprehending characteristics and resolute belief cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas distancing can sever them, we know that there is a distinction among the three types of wisdom regarding the severing [of afflictions].

Regarding the severing of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*), wisdom is called "severing" because it suppresses them; if one refers to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the path capable of severing is [the untainted path].
Regarding the delusions, as stated in the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning):

"The section states that according to one interpretation, based on reality, those who have first subdued them [subdue] the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) to subdue the nine grades of delusion.

The first three types of mental attention subdue the first two grades; the fourth type of mental attention subdues the middle three grades; and the final three types of mental attention subdue the latter three grades."

In the *Abhidharma* treatises, it is stated that those first two types of attention (*manasikāra*) have not yet been able to suppress or exhaust the afflictions of the three categories; therefore, they are called "not severing the afflictions.
This does not mean that these two types of attention do not sever the first two categories of worldly [afflictions], as explained in the *Arthapradīpa*.
Section. Regarding the phrase "if one observes until there is neither longing nor aversion": among the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), the first six also involve longing and aversion;

however, when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one does not employ longing and aversion. Therefore, those [six] are not taken as the preparatory application (*prayoga*). This is to be understood as being the same as before.

Section. Regarding "the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) is able to suppress" and "because it is immediately followed by the untainted (*anāsrava*)": this refers to the fact that the tainted preparatory practice preceding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is able to suppress the afflictions;
it is said in terms of immediate succession that this is immediately followed by the untainted path of seeing.
Section. Regarding the phrase "up to the stage of applied practice (*prayoga*) within the path with outflows (*sāsrava*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

Prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), during the distant stage of the path with outflows, one has not yet extensively subdued [the afflictions]; therefore, this is not yet the stage of having attained applied practice. Having further refined [the mind] thereafter, one attains the state of applied practice.
Alternatively, some manuscripts read "various" (*pṛthak*) or "extensive" (*vistara*). The reading "extensive" (*vistara*) should be correct; one should further consult other manuscripts.

Section. Regarding the statement that one may also attain uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) preparatory practice (*prayoga*) at a later time: this refers to the period following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Section. As for the fact that preparatory knowledge itself possesses four paths: within the Bodhisattva’s uncontaminated path of preparation, there are indeed four paths, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), Chapter Ten, along with its commentary.
Section: Regarding the statement that "among the four paths, one naturally penetrates the three wisdoms," this means generally that the four paths can penetrate the three wisdoms;

it does not mean that the three wisdoms exist within the four paths of preparatory application (*prayoga*). These three wisdoms are precisely the fundamental (*mūla*), the subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*), and the preparatory (*prayoga*) wisdoms.

Section: Regarding the statement that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward there are four paths, these refer to the four paths within both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

From the eighth stage upward, the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) is absent. If this is so, how can there be a path of application? In terms of its functional meaning (*artha*), it is said that the wisdom of application exists;
in terms of its substantial entity (*svabhāva*), it is said that it does not exist.

Section. What prevents hearing and reflection from also being able to sever and suppress [afflictions]? Since it is established by definition that there are two types—those consisting of hearing and those consisting of reflection—what prevents it from being established by definition that hearing and reflection can sever delusions?

Section. Furthermore, regarding that which is "not based on authoritative scripture": the meanings within this treatise may appear to contradict various teachings; thus, it is termed "not based on authoritative scripture.

It does not mean that what is spoken by non-sages is termed "not based on authoritative scripture. This is an error resulting from the scribe’s misreading of the character for "food" (食) as "attachment" (執).
It was a clerical mistake.

Section. Regarding the statement that "the Mahāyāna is ultimately able to sever all afflictions" and so forth: there is no text in the Mahāyāna that explicitly prescribes the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as the means for severing afflictions.

While the name "foundation of dharma-mindfulness" (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is general, according to the underlying principle, it is through attaining this foundation of dharma-mindfulness that one severs afflictions.

Within the Hīnayāna school, the foundation of dharma-mindfulness is defined as taking the Four Noble Truths as its collective object; one contemplates the reality of suffering and regards it as suffering. Now, in the Mahāyāna...

When one contemplates suffering and so forth through the vehicle [of the Mahāyāna], it is neither suffering nor non-suffering; because one does not fixate determinately upon any single [aspect], it is called "comprehensive" (*sāmānya*), which differs from that [former approach].

Therefore, in the chapter [it is said]: "Thus, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth, up to 'therefore they are not contradictory'"; since these [factors] such as emptiness take the comprehensive as their object and are able to sever the afflictions, [they are effective].

The chapter states: "The mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) takes [all objects] collectively as its object and eliminates afflictions without error. It is not the case that only [the mindfulness of suffering] would result in contradiction. This means that it is not incorrect to call collective observation "mindfulness of phenomena.

Unlike the Hīnayāna schools, which take suffering and so forth as real suffering and so forth, the Mahāyāna universally establishes [phenomena] through conventional designation; therefore, no contradiction arises.
If one does not take non-conceptualization (*apratiṣṭhāna*) as a collective object, there is an absence of non-conceptualization.
[The] Chapter states: "Faith penetrates the side of the untainted and abandons the delusions regarding phenomena. Question: Why is it that only the two sides of faith are explained? Answer:
The clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of that morality is subsumed under the factor of morality within the Eightfold Path. Furthermore, prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), there is no [pure] morality;

thus, the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are not confused with it. It does not distinguish the four kinds of unshakable faith (*avekṣā*). That is to say, in the stage of untainted preparation (*anāsrava-prayoga*), faith is the root.
Because it exists in both places, it is said to "pervade the untainted. Since the intention is to take both, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* take the subsequently attained [wisdom].
Wisdom is termed "wisdom of the limit" (*antya-jñāna*); therefore, it is said to "sever delusions. This distinguishes it from contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*), which is designated as the "limit.

If the *Abhidharma* intends to take contaminated conventional wisdom as the "wisdom of the limit," this accords with the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school. This shall be further analyzed below in the discussion on contemplation.

Section. Regarding the phrase "those who are currently subduing the afflictions" (*kleśa*), in the Mahāyāna, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) serves as the proximate practice (*upacāra*) capable of subduing the afflictions, while wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and signlessness (*animitta*) serve as the remote preparatory applications (*prayoga*).
If one is a follower of the Hīnayāna who contemplates the principle of the Four Noble Truths, all three types [of samādhis] function as preparatory applications.

It subdues [the afflictions] differently from the Mahāyāna; when the distant and the near are combined, one may say it penetrates all three practices. Alternatively, it is said that the practitioners of the two vehicles contemplate the Four Noble Truths and subdue [afflictions] through the practice of emptiness.

Section. Regarding the various differing explanations found within Mahāyāna texts: these are the assertions made by the [authorities] below, as well as those stated in the various treatises (*śāstra*).

Section. As for the statement that "the eight aspects (*ākāra*) are signless (*animitta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*"): the four aspects of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) can perform the contemplation of signlessness; therefore, they are called "signless.
However, the intention of the present contemplation refers exclusively to the tainted (*sāsrava*), which is designated as "signs" (*nimitta*). Since the Path is untainted, it is not [so designated].
"Mutually inclusive.
Regarding the passage "The threefold path of the fourfold penetration": this refers to the penetration of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Regarding the passage "Because the substance of the two natures is not fixed": these correspond respectively to wishlessness, signlessness, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The two natures [are established] because they correspond to the Four Truths.

Regarding the chapter on the three gates, it says: "As for the principle that the three natures all universally penetrate [the truth], one should consult the eighth [chapter]. Question: There is the emptiness of the two—birth and phenomena; there is the emptiness of the three gates of liberation;
within the Four Truths, there is the specific emptiness under the Truth of Suffering, and there is the general emptiness of the common object of the Four Truths. These four...

What is the difference between [the emptiness of] space and [the emptiness of] self and phenomena? Answer: The two types of emptiness—of self and of phenomena—are able to observe both self and phenomena;

because they refer to "self" and "phenomena," they universally observe the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This is because within both the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there exist the two principles of arising and phenomena.

Regarding the gate of liberation that is emptiness, since it universally observes the three natures of self and phenomena, the specific emptiness within the category of suffering is able to observe the non-existence within suffering, while the contemplation of non-self observes the self, and the contemplation of emptiness observes [emptiness].
"Mine" (*mama*) refers to the emptiness of the four truths as a whole; it is the practice of universally contemplating the selflessness of the four truths. Question:

Regarding the two types of emptiness (*dvi-śūnyatā*), one further contemplates the four truths; how does this differ from the "emptiness of the whole" (*piṇḍa-śūnyatā*)? Answer: The "emptiness of the whole" is a collective contemplation that does not differentiate between arising phenomena (*jāti-dharma*) and established phenomena (*bhāva-dharma*).

The two types of emptiness involve individual contemplations, and are thus distinct. Alternatively, it is said that the practice of emptiness merely empties "mine" and does not encompass "selflessness"; however, the gateway of the two types of emptiness is comprehensive.

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) also encompasses two types. The gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*) is the distant preparatory stage (*dūra-prayoga*), whereas the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) constitute the proximate preparatory stage (*āsanna-prayoga*).

Therefore, when the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) manifests, one establishes even a slight object as being the nature of consciousness; this is precisely what constitutes the proximate preparatory stage.
Since that [stage] is not termed the "two emptinesses," it differs from the gate of emptiness. Alternatively, it may be identical to the gate of emptiness, for it is indeed the two emptinesses.

Therefore, the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) serves as the remote preparation (*dūraprayoga*), which is itself the bliss. This is because, among the three preceding gates, emptiness is specifically taken as the proximate preparation (*āsannaprayoga*).

Question: But when the two types of emptiness are established, do they not also sever their respective referents (*vācya*)? Answer: If they are correctly established, they are merely cognitive understandings (*jñāna-avabodha*).
These cognitions differ in their characteristics; for now, we rely on the designators (*vācaka*). This is because, based on these cognitions, true suchness (*tathatā*) has not yet been realized.
Because it has not yet attained nirvāṇa. If one were to concede this characteristic, it would then be explaining the ultimate meaning;

however, even the understanding of the two kinds of emptiness—the suchness and the wisdom—is still merely the arising of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), as it has not yet been realized through contemplation. Thus, even the "truth" included within the gate of realization is subsumed under that fourth category of the conventional. Question:
Regarding the small object present before one, this emptiness possesses a corresponding aspect; it is distinguished by the mental faculty into separate objective portions.

Does this mean that two understandings arise upon a single aspect? Answer: Because two understandings arise upon a single aspect. If that is so, since this is called "non-conceptual," how can two understandings arise?
Answer: At that time, it is also treated as a non-conceptual understanding; thus, by virtue of being non-conceptual, it becomes conceptual.
Upon reaching the subsequent stage, one immediately realizes non-attainment; only then does the transformation into non-conceptuality occur.
Regarding the first chapter, from "The Bodhisattva of the First Kalpa" up to "regarding non-exertion as supreme":
a beginner may be born into the higher realms by means of the six practices, whereas one who has long practiced need not rely on the six practices to be born there.

Chapter. Regarding the statement that a śrāvaka of sharp faculties reaches up to the eighty-eighth fetter: Question: Since it is admitted that a single path exhausts all afflictions, does one still perform the remaining fifteen paths? Answer:
It is admitted that the others do not further sever afflictions, as they serve the purpose of contemplative practice; therefore, they must be performed in their entirety.

There are those of the Sarvāstivāda school who leap over the middle two fruits and proceed directly to the fourth fruit; this applies to those from the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception downwards.

There are various afflictions (*kleśa*). Within the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), having already abandoned and realized them in their entirety, one gives rise to contaminated acquisitions (*sāsravaprāpti*);

subsequently, because one intends to give rise to their uncontaminated acquisitions (*anāsravaprāpti*), this case is also similar. Among the twenty schools (*nikāya*), it is not known which school maintains [this view]; certainly, it is not the Sarvāstivāda school.
Eighty-eight: According to the Hīnayāna school, there are eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) when the four truths (*satya*) of the three realms (*dhātu*) are analyzed.

In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), each truth has ten; in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), each has seven. This excludes two views from the upper two realms’ truths.
Furthermore, below each truth in those upper realms, one instance of hatred (*dveṣa*) is additionally excluded. This can be understood by reflecting upon it.
Section. Regarding the statement that "the false reaches [the true] by means of its true form, yet it is not said to have categories": because the form is true, it receives the name "false";

however, the essence of the false is without categories. It is not that the true itself lacks categories; rather, categories are falsely projected upon it, and thus it is also called "without categories."

Regarding the passage, "The three *kalpas* are severed moment by moment," this master maintains that while the afflictions (*kleśa*) are eliminated in distinct categories, there is no differentiation as to their quantity;
rather, he speaks of them collectively as being severed moment by moment.

Section. That it is not so today: the ancient masters stated that there are nine grades (*navaprakāra*), yet they did not distinguish which [afflictions] are extinguished or by what means they are eliminated;
therefore, their view is untenable.

Section. Regarding the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) up to only the ninth grade: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) offers two interpretations concerning each stage (*bhūmi*).
Within this, there are nine grades; these should be understood by examining that [text].
Chapter One: From the eighty-first up to the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is likewise so. One subdues those eighty-one grades of afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Section. Some say there is no chapter [on this]. Consider that, in comparison, it is somewhat difficult to permeate [the seeds].
Section. Regarding the explanation of the second grasping: among the eight consciousnesses counted in reverse order, the eighth is the first and the seventh is the second.

Alternatively, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the sixth consciousness is taken as the first grasping and the seventh consciousness as the second grasping. However, I have not yet seen [this explicitly stated].
Regarding the passage from the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayaguhya-śāstra* (Renwang jing) stating that "form is coarse and mind is subtle": the former two stages both encompass the manifest and the seeds;

the obstructions to omniscience (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also termed afflictions (*kleśa*). The latter two stages refer exclusively to the manifest [afflictions] within the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It does not arise; therefore, the seventh consciousness is omitted for the most part and not discussed.

Alternatively, although the seeds are actually severed during the first two stages, it is stated that only the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are addressed while their seeds are not taken into account. As for the phrase "the same applies to the arising of afflictions," there are two types:
first, regarding the four preceding stages, all were explained in terms of seeds; now, stating that the active manifestations are likewise [treated] as seeds is called... [name].

The same applies to the stage of abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhūmi*). Regarding the two types of birth, although the preceding four stages clarify only the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), here it is stated that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise the same as those.
When viewed through the lens of deluded sentiment, the afflictions appear to be predominant. The reason for this is that in the latter two stages, there are no active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Alternatively, it is said that all four types are subsumed under the latencies (*vāsanā*); one should examine this according to the distinction between the coarse and the subtle.
The Sūtra and its Commentary further state that "gradual progression" explains the reason for the divisions of the chapters.

Regarding the phrase "also able to permanently sever a small portion of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*"): this refers to the severing of the birth of the obscuration of meditative absorption (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*) and the ability to suppress it, whereby one attains ultimate non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is termed "permanent severance," yet it does not mean the actual eradication of the seeds of those obscurations.
Section. Regarding "the remaining [stages] up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are indeterminate across nine stages": this refers generally to the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
Excluding the Desire Realm, in the remaining eight stages, the number of defilements abandoned is indeterminate according to how many are actually severed. This is called an Anāgāmin (Non-returner).
Section: Regarding the selection of two fruits, these are the first and the fourth. This is explained in detail in the second chapter of the *Dīpa*. Section:

Now, as for the Bodhisattva who "subdues" and "attains" the fruit through meditative concentration (*samādhi*): attaining that concentration is called "attaining concentration," while being born in that place is called "attaining the fruit.
This refers to one who possesses the initial karma of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), and who, by means of the six modes of practice, delights in birth [in those realms].
That stage is either produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or by the force of karma; it is not produced through aspiration.

Regarding the statement that "the obstacle (*āvaraṇa*) and the karmic fruit (*karmaphala*) are severed in different paths": the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) severs the obstacle, while the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) severs the karmic fruit.

In reality, the uninterrupted path has already severed the karmic fruit; however, because it prevents [its recurrence], it is said to be in the path of liberation. One should consult the third chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding this liberation.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "lying prostrate in the eighth stage," this refers to the six consciousnesses.

Regarding the phrase "abandoning what was previously practiced—namely other concentrations—and entering the concentrations of other vehicles," abandoning the superior for the inferior is termed [this].
Obstruction. Since abandoning the inferior and adopting the superior is not an obstruction, it is not so classified.

Regarding the phrase "the objective basis upon which conceptualization arises": by means of the first three [obstructions], the substantial entities that serve as the bases and objects of that [conceptualization] arise;
the other two should be understood accordingly.

Section: Regarding the principle that [afflictions] are common to both the abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), although the text speaks of "cultivation," it refers to the principle that they are common to both seeing and cultivation.
Section: Regarding the eight afflictions of the impure stages and the nine afflictions of the pure stages:

the seven stages prior to the eighth are called the impure stages, because the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) within the six consciousnesses are admitted to manifest there. The final three stages are called the pure stages, because the two obstacles within the six consciousnesses are permanently... [eliminated].

They do not function in a state of prostration. Regarding the seventh object of knowledge (*jñeya*), its arising occurs at various times; it will not be discussed here in detail for fear of being too brief. If that is so, how does the seventh differ [from the others]? Answer:

The seventh relies on conventional designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*) and is exclusively cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). If one speaks of the two kinds of names, they do not mention cultivation, because such is the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
Otherwise, by what other name could one designate them as pure or impure? It is stated that the remaining seven penetrate the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Regarding the cultivation of the path, it is said in general that the preceding seven [mental applications] pertain to both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in stating that each individual consciousness does not necessarily pervade both paths.
In the seventh chapter, concerning "entering the fundamental [dhyāna]," it is stated that all seven mental applications of cultivation pervade the fundamental stages. One interpretation says:

while the six preceding [applications] are said to rely on the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) because they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), the seventh pertains to the fundamental stage; however, if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), all seven [pervade the fundamental stages].
This refers to the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of all types.

Regarding the passage: "Furthermore, there are minds that are dissociated from latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and minds that are not dissociated from latent dispositions," those dissociated from latent dispositions are precisely the counteractive paths (*pratipakṣamārga*).
This teaching also describes [the state where] [defilements] have been abandoned and do not coalesce, both being present simultaneously.
Section: Regarding "equality," it refers to the fact that the subject and object of cultivation arise and cease together in equal measure. Section:

The phrase "the method of contemplating the severance of delusions as in the Ten Stages" is cited as an illustrative proof; for although it involves a contemplation of arising, it does not sever arising.
Alternatively, this [case] is also like that.

Section: Regarding the fact that specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are neither identical to nor different from all general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): this means that the specific characteristics of form (*rūpa*) and so forth are neither identical to nor different from general characteristics such as impermanence (*anityatā*).
Section. Regarding "each being individually realized": this clarifies that the internal [realization] refers to that very *dharmatā*. Section.

"That which can universally serve as the two contemplations capable of severing" refers to the contemplation that takes both general and specific objects. Based on the realization, one abides in each individual practice.
"Exposition" refers to the contemplations of *vijñaptimātra*, selflessness, and so forth; "realization" refers to [the fact that] regarding the true principle of each and every phenomenon...
This is because it can be known.
Chapter: By practicing these two—namely, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Chapter:

Regarding the phrase "subsequently attaining the obstacles to mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth," this refers to the fact that by distancing oneself from the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) and so on, one now attains the Dharma.
This cannot be known by mere chance; it can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the three provisional practices for each of the two truths, as explained in the chapter on "Increase and Decrease" below, I have not recorded them here to avoid prolixity.
Section. What is meant by the fourth being also called "established" (*prajñapti*)? These two modes of emptiness differ from the preceding three;

their characteristics are such that they can be compared to what is attained rather than being designated as "established. Nevertheless, they are also provisionally termed "non-established. This distinction in meaning should be understood through reflection.

Section. Alternatively, "worldly" (*loka*) refers to the mundane. "Worldly" is the general term, while "mundane" (*sāṃvṛta*) signifies the meaning of the conduct manifested upon that which is generally established.

Alternatively, it is said that "worldly" means that which is subject to destruction, while "mundane" refers to the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Or, "worldly" refers to the provisional (*prajñapti*), while "secular" (*sāṃvṛta*) refers to the essence of phenomena.

Section. Regarding "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*): "conventional" refers to the essential nature of conventional phenomena; "truth" (*satya*) refers to the meaning of reality within that essential nature.
Alternatively, "conventional" is a general term for the four [noble truths], while "truth" is a specific name for each of those four. Their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are difficult to discern.
Why are all four considered conventional? Because "truth" is precisely their specific name.
Regarding the passage, "The abandonment of the means of expression to discuss the ultimate meaning is not an objective realm," this implies that the nature [of reality] is supreme;
it is only when it is not taken as an object of delusion that it receives the name "supreme. This is identical to the three types of supreme truths mentioned previously.
Section: "The Sublime Transcends All Dharmas. Question: The fourth noble truth is also a transcendence beyond all dharmas; would its name not then be confused with the former? Answer:

The previous statement regarding "transcendence" was made in relation to the three preceding conventional truths; the subsequent statement regarding "transcendence" is made in contrast to the three preceding true truths.
Therefore, there is no error.
Section: Regarding the "truth of ultimate reality" (*paramārtha-satya*), it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound based on the preceding [section on] conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Section: Alternatively, regarding the phrase "either lacking substantiality" or "the substance is non-existent," this refers to the mutual absence [of entities]; there is no other meaning.
Regarding the "chapters" and their "bases": the Four Noble Truths are taken as the bases for these chapters.
Regarding the "self-explanations of the Two Vehicles": these are the doctrines discussed within their own respective schools.
