If one were to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, it would not be like the five or eight [precepts], which are merely similar.
Section. Regarding the statement that "those who would otherwise have no way to reach hell can be subsumed therein": hell can only be subsumed within the Bodhisattva precepts.

However, while it is generally a place where mixed [karmic] retributions are experienced, according to our current interpretation, it may also be possible to receive them in a purely [exclusive] state of retribution; what harm is there in this? This is due to the power of the Buddha and others.
As for the mention of "purely receiving," this is stated with reference to other times.

Section. [The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] prohibits both [the taking of refuge and the precepts] for humans, but does not prohibit [them for] animals and so forth. The intent of this treatise is as follows:
since the destinies of animals and so forth are not prohibited [from taking refuge], why should they be unable to receive the upāsaka precepts? The character "俱" (*jù*, "both") is likely an error.
Chapter. Regarding the roots that serve as the basis for the arousal of afflictions leading to transgression: the "roots" refer to the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Taking these roots as a basis, they are able to arouse the seeds of afflictions leading to transgression. The initial *anāgamya* (preparatory) concentration is able to counteract them. Some say:

The character "gen" (根) is an error; it should be combined with the following to form the character "zong" (總). The section concerning the establishment of the counteragent based on the seeds of afflictions that constitute the violation of precepts states:

"By the nature of things (*dharmatā*), all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are able to suppress [the afflictions]. This is not correct; it is not the case that every meditative concentration is capable of suppressing them, nor is it the case that only this specific meditative concentration can suppress the violation of precepts.

Section. As for the claim that only the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possesses this [discipline] and that it is therefore untenable: if there were a fixed discipline (*dharma-śīla*) in the form realm, such a principle would indeed be untenable.
However, if one maintains the position that there is a fixed precept (*niyata-śīla*), then because there is matter (*rūpa*) in the form realm, it exists only within the form realm.

Regarding the passage, "There are those who cultivate only the path," etc.: the previous statement that the six stages constitute the general rule was made because the author of the treatise wished to clarify that even in the three lower formless realms, [the cultivation of the path] is possible.

Therefore, he again introduces the term "there are" (*yǒu*) to raise this inquiry. Now, observing the flow of the text, it would also be better logically if the two characters "yǒu-yì" (meaning "there is a principle") were not present, as their presence disrupts the sequence.

Section. Regarding the phrase "the stage of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-bhūmi*)... up to the meaning of 'clearly severed' (*vidita-prahāṇa-artha*)," the character *ming* (明) should properly be the character *de* (得).

This explains that in that stage of non-perception, there is only the meaning of "attaining" (*prāpti*) a partial severance (*dūra-bhāga-prahāṇa*); it is not [actual] severance. Severance is defined as the name for "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).

The characters "meaning of attaining severance" (*prahāṇa-prāpti-artha*) belong to the stage of non-perception. If the "meaning of clearly severed" were to belong to what follows below, then logically it would be contradictory. [This concerns] form (*rūpa*).

The meaning of "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) regarding the body belonging to a particular realm (*dhātu*) contradicts the principle of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). This is because one must first abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of a lower realm before being born into a higher one.

Once the body has been born there, the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have already been abandoned; how, then, could the body belonging to the two upper realms possess the status of being "abandoned"?
Therefore, we know that the body merely attains "remoteness" (*dūratā*); this is why it cannot be said to belong to the lower realm.
Section: Regarding the statement that "the bodies of all three realms can all arise," this text provides a general overview.

While the bodies of the two upper realms can only give rise to [defilements] of the remote category (*viprakṛṣṭa-bhāga*), based on a body of the desire realm, they can arise across all categories. This may be understood through reflection.

Section. Regarding the phrase "the intention to manifest [virtue] and so forth, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*)," this refers to what was previously explained as the "middle of the middles" (*madhyamadhyama*).

It is the position that allows for the existence of untainted discipline within the intermediate category of discipline (*madhyama-śīla*), according to the interpretation of the Master. Section. Regarding the phrase "arising" and below, this clarifies that various types of discipline (*saṃvara*) arise in accordance with the various realms of existence (*gati*).
As for the word "therefore" (*hi*), it serves as a topical marker (*uddeśa*).

Section. Regarding the phrase "distinct liberation of the three realms": the character "shuo" (to speak) is an error; it should be the character "tuo" (liberation). "Distinct liberation of the three realms" refers to the Bodhisattva precepts. Why is this?

The precept for gathering wholesome dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) means that all wholesome dharmas—both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)—within the three realms are the distinct liberations through which the Bodhisattva gathers wholesome dharmas.
What is the reason for the subsequent mention of "skillful speech"? Next, it mentions "concentration" (*samādhi*).

Regarding the paths and the untainted (*anāsrava*): this applies to the general exposition of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). As for the distinct liberation from the three realms, it refers specifically to the Bodhisattva precepts. Reflect further on this chapter:

all these are capable of reaching that which is produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). That is to say, the form of the untainted and other types of restraint (*saṃvara-rūpa*) is what produces them;
they are produced by the four great elements that constitute the body and speech of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Section. As for the statement that "one is already called a 'doer' once the boundary [of the act] has been established," this meaning is erroneous and redundant, and therefore useless. Section.

Regarding the claim that "the Hīnayāna necessarily possesses the characteristic of ultimate knowledge, and thus one becomes a killer," the Hīnayāna teaches that when ghosts and spirits see the body and speech of those sages, they manifest expressions of anger;
it is only through the exertion of such verbal expression that killing is carried out. Therefore, there is [a distinction] above.
[The section on] "Manifesting the unmanifest.
Regarding the Mahāyāna position that "intention manifests up to the point of initiating the unmanifest of killing": "Unmanifest" means there is no bodily or vocal manifestation.
[The section on] "If it were not so, how could it be established?": If the mental karma of a rishi also exists, it nonetheless depends upon bodily and vocal manifestations.
Therefore, it can be seen that this contradicts the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Regarding the passage in the *Chapters* (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī) which states, "Now, to explain why this is not the intention of that treatise: 'not employing bodily action' means that the rishi did not kill the people of the country with his body;
'the instrument of killing' refers to the rishi manifesting his anger, at which time his physical appearance changed."

It is moving. The words that issue forth are sounds of resentment; these are all instruments of killing. Since these instruments of killing do not themselves produce matter (*rūpa*), the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) born of intention also receives the name "matter.
The original intent of that treatise does not speak of mental action (*manas-karman*); rather, it speaks by relying on manifest action (*vijñapti*).

As for the phrase "by which one previously becomes a hungry ghost," this accords with the intent of that treatise. The intent of that treatise is simply that [the result] arises through mental conduct.
One becomes a killing-demon (*kravyāda*). Since one does not perform the act of killing oneself, it is said that the mental karma lacks the manifest expressions (*vijñapti*) of body and speech.

This is based on the fact that one becomes a sinful demon from the outset; however, while the spirits and demons have not yet killed [the victim], the sage’s path of action (*karmapatha*) has likewise not been attained. It is only upon the actual killing that it is attained.
Section. Regarding the *śaṇḍha* (eunuch) and *paṇḍaka* (impotent): the former is grave, while the latter is light. Section.
Regarding the "heretical thief-dweller" (*tīrthika-caura-vāsika*): one who falsely pretends to be a bhikṣu is called a heretical thief-dweller.

If, at the time of receiving the precepts, conditions such as the necessary requisites are not fulfilled, although one has received them, one does not obtain the precepts. Yet, dwelling among the bhikṣus, one participates in the *poṣadha* and other communal rites; this is termed [the heretical thief-dweller].
The case of one who dwells as a thief (a *caura-vāsin*) may be understood by analogy.

According to the Chapter [on Offenses]: if one dwells separately [from the community], one commits the four root offenses. To immediately confess without concealment is termed "breaking the precepts" (*dauḥśīlya*).
Yet, one does not incur a root offense. Because there was no disclosure, one undergoes *parivāsa* (probation) and performs repentance for the rest of one's life;

therefore, it is explained separately as being distinct from the [other] non-common [offenses]. Some say this refers to receiving the precepts with a mind of theft while residing in a different *saṃgha*; this too is untenable.
Section. Regarding those who do not live in communion: if one commits a root offense and does not immediately confess it, [they are excluded].
Section. If one is detested by the king, the king shall confiscate their family estate.
Section. If there is that which constitutes an improper act—an improper act being one that violates the King’s teachings.
Section. If it is drawn away by another kalpa, or seized by another, even if it has already been completed as theft, it is subsequently transferred to another person.

That which others obtain is called "obtained by another. Some say that *kṣetra* means the drawing forth of the formation of an eon (*kalpa-saṃvarta*), while "obtained by another" means having completed the act of theft.
Although this constitutes one interpretation, it contains many divergent points and does not equal the previous explanation.
Section. If one follows the five precepts, the first is what is termed "receiving the five precepts.

Section. Regarding those who merely observe the prohibitive precepts (*śīla-virati*): remove the initial character "prohibitive" (*zhē*). When receiving the ten precepts, one obtains the prohibitive precepts as a category;
the remaining four follow along with it.

Section. Regarding the statement "if one damages [the precepts] to the point of reaching [the ultimate], it is sudden and so forth": the three branches and four branches do not refer to each other individually;
rather, at the very moment the initial precept is received, it may be termed "sudden. As for the term "cutting" (chan), this is based on their mutual relationship.

Section. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the five precepts of the bhikṣuṇī," the character "five" (五) is an error; it should be the character "complete" (具). The intent of this objection is as follows:
when receiving the complete precepts (upasaṃpadā), four branches are first obtained; yet when relinquishing the complete precepts, one only relinquishes three—does one also relinquish all four?
Section. Regarding the phrase "generally relinquishing the seven branches, etc.": Question: Although it is said that one receives [the precepts] individually, this merely increases their clarity;

they are not explained separately again. Why is it that at the time of relinquishment, all seven are relinquished? Answer: When it says "relinquishing three," the seven branches are relinquished in their entirety; as for the four branches, they are cited according to what is relinquished.

This is explained for the sake of clarification; it does not mean that the essence [of the precepts] is abandoned. Since the ten precepts are obtained at the time of receiving them, they are abandoned when those ten are relinquished.

If that is so regarding their abandonment, why is it said that when the six dharmas are abandoned, one abandons the four essences? Answer: In the undertaking of the six dharmas, there are no separate dharmas other than these;

one merely maintains the first four, just as in the case of the sevenfold ritual of undertaking the karma. Therefore, when the six dharmas are abandoned, the four essences—the full precepts—are abandoned. This relies upon the Great Saṃgha.

The ritual procedure for what has been received is distinct and differs from the ritual procedure for the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*). For this reason, it merely relinquishes the functions of the four bases (*catur-vastu*).

A Dharma Master provides an explanation to clarify this: "At the time of receiving the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), one may obtain the four bases as distinct entities because the ritual procedures for the six dharmas (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) are separate.
The six dharmas and the ten precepts are received solely by nuns; they cannot produce full ordination. One must rely on the [full] ordination [to do so]."
When a monk receives [the precepts], he requests the ordination from his teacher and performs it once more. Why, then, would one not separately obtain the four bases [of morality]?

Thus we know that there is no logical error in obtaining them separately. If they were obtained separately, then when one relinquishes the full set of precepts (*upasampadā*), one would relinquish those bases as well.
Section. The commentary states, "up to the point where seeds can induce [retribution]. Question: By what principle are seeds able to induce *vipāka* (ripened fruit)? Answer:
That which supports contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma is termed "inducing. Question: If even the manifest state (*pravṛtti*) cannot yet summon it, how can the seed induce it? Answer:
Speaking in terms of actual manifestation, the manifest state is also capable of inducing it; however, because the karma has not yet matured, the fruit does not arise immediately.

Therefore, it perfumes and forms seeds, which later bring about results. If this is so, since the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) itself can bring about [results], why is there a need for seeds to produce them?

Answer: Although the active manifestation arises, because it perishes moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*), it perfumes the seeds, and subsequently the result is produced from those seeds. If there were only the active manifestation, [it could not produce a future result].

After the active manifestation has ceased, the subsequent fruit arises; since the co-existent cause has long since perished, it is for this reason that one speaks of the "seed" as being what brings about [the result].

The seeds of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path are so called because they belong to the categories of concentration and the Path; they are designated as "concentration" and "Path" only figuratively. This is not like other people who take these seeds to be the actual substantial essence (*dravya-svabhāva*) of the precepts of concentration and the Path.
Section. If [the action] is not produced, then body and speech are not produced. Section.
If, as previously stated, it is the bodily karma that is primary, this implies that the sage’s intention—his mental karma—is what is heavy, for he was capable of killing the people of the nation.
If one follows the first interpretation, which allows for the existence of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*), then because such manifest karma exists...
The people of the country were in the process of dying; this is precisely manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*). Why, then, do you say that the mental [action] is predominant?

Regarding the passage stating "the explanation is that it is also matter (*rūpa*)," this means that from the rain of stones sent forth by those spirits, the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) of the rishis acquires the designation of "matter.
It is a provisional name for "one's own matter" based on what was sent forth by others.
Section. Regarding the practitioner who maintains the seven types of undertaken karma (*samātta-śīla*):

[this] sets aside the *Śāstra*. Section. Now, as for the statement that the substance of the ten karmas is volition (*cetanā*): Question. What is the distinction between the paths of action (*karmapatha*) and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)? Answer. The substance of karma is truly volition;
that which is non-informative matter is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Because it prevents unwholesome physical form, it is metaphorically named "non-informative matter."
Furthermore, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is the superior capacity planted [by the manifest], which is the actual substance of the volition of action (*karmacetanā*).

Moreover, one who has not yet received the precepts but merely abstains from killing attains only one type of path of action (*karmapatha*) by its own nature; once the precepts have been received, one further separately attains that unmanifest morality (*śīla-avijñapti*).

Furthermore, regarding the wholesome [action] of the middle way, although there is non-informative action (*avijñapti*) even without it being derived from formal undertaking (*samādāna*), in terms of its essential nature and function, it is not identical to the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Question: Is the essence of the precept merely a functional capacity upon the seeds (*bīja*), and if so, is it provisional (*prajñapti*) or substantial (*dravya*)? Answer: It is provisional.

If that is so, since provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) are like non-existence, how can the sutras state that precepts (*śīla*) can produce results? Furthermore, why is it said that upholding them is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*)?

Answer: It is the actual seeds (*bīja*) that can produce results. Because the essence of the seed is designated according to its function, it is called "precepts producing results. As for the term "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*):
This is also stated according to its substance (*tattva*). To say it is "neither form nor mind" is to describe its functional capacity (*śakti*). Question:

If the substance of volition (*cetanā*) is karma, and that which has the capacity to induce [rebirth] is merely that karma, what then is actual morality (*śīla*)? Answer: It is simply one and the same thing; the names differ only based on its specific meaning and function. Question:

Since morality is a distinct functional capacity upon the seed (*bīja*), does the eighth consciousness take it as an object (*ālambana*)? Answer: It does not take it as an object. If that is so, [how is it maintained]?
Question: How can the vast and great capacity of the seeds itself serve as the object of cognition? Answer:

Because "vastness" is substantial (*dravya*) while "precept" (*śīla*) is nominal (*prajñapti*), one takes its substance as the object of cognition, not its nominality. Question: Within a single capacity, what is the distinction between the nominal and the substantial? Answer:

Vastness arises directly from the seeds and does not depend on the prevention of external factors; thus it is called the substantial body of the precept (*śīlatattva*). Its form, however, externally prevents [transgressions of] body and speech; therefore—
It is a nominal designation (*prajñapti*). This is because it is likewise excluded [from being a real entity], just as in the case of "Dittha" and so forth.
Consider this. Regarding the question, "How can one say that it extends to non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?"—the intended meaning of the answer is:
what fault is there in establishing the name based on the color of rain and stones produced by a nominal designation?
In the chapter [on] "Those Born Now," the two characters "yi" (亦) and "zhe" (者) are misplaced; they should be combined with the character "zai" (在).
In the chapter [on] "All First Following a Teacher," the character "shou" (受) is missing beneath the character "shi" (師).
Chapter on Homage (Volume Four, Part Two).
Therefore, regarding the phrase "I bow my head to the Great Śramaṇa," the verse states: "Bowing my head is not merely physical homage.

If that is so, how does the statement in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*—"How is it that 'paying homage' (namas-kṛ-) applies to both body and speech?"—be explained? Answer: In the commentary of that treatise, it says "body" itself...
Regarding verbal action, there is no place for its explanation in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. For now, based on the extant text, it is judged as follows:

according to the actual similarity [of the passage], the "turning of the fruit of craving" refers to body and mind being called the "fruit of craving"; because one turns toward and moves within the fruit of craving through a virtuous mind, one performs prostration.
"Respect. "Chapter.
Regarding the general designation for *kṣānti* (patience/endurance): *Kṣānti* alone does not refer to bowing with body and mind;

rather, "bowing" (*kṣānti*) is a specific name for bodily action (*kāyakarman*), and it is also a general term for the three types of action (*trikarman*). For now, *kṣānti* is treated according to its specific [meaning].
This is explained according to its name; in reality, however, it applies to all three.

As for the statement that "it also applies to seeds as appropriate," these two types of unmanifest karma—bodily and vocal—are established based on the seeds of volition (*cetanā*), and thus take those seeds as their essence.
Section. Regarding the two karmas of body and speech reaching the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*): next, the nature of the homage paid to the state of Buddhahood is clarified;

it may also reside in the two spheres of form (*rūpa*) and sound. Since the state of Buddhahood possesses the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and matter (*rūpa*) of the karmas of body and speech, it thus pervades four spheres.
The meaning of the present text is that the unmanifest matter of the two karmas of body and speech, and so forth, are therefore collectively explained by their various names and categories.
As for the reason why one should reflect upon this chapter on verbal action and ritual,
all contradictions and obstacles have been addressed in the Chapter on the Three Wheels and its commentary; therefore, they will not be explained further here.
Section Two: On the Extensiveness of the Objects of Refuge and Reverence. Question: A distinction may be made between reverence and refuge when directed toward a narrow object;

however, what is the difference between reverence and refuge when directed toward a broad object? Answer: Refuge is broad, whereas reverence is not necessarily so; therefore, these two are distinguished. It is not the case that broad reverence is identical to refuge.
The reason refuge in the Triple Gem is broad is that it encompasses all [beings]. Although reverence may be directed toward three [objects], it is not [necessarily] universal in its scope.
This is broad [in scope]. Furthermore, it is entirely distinct.

Regarding the "four branches" and "seven branches" and so forth: as for the term "branches," the four branches of vocal action refer specifically to vocal manifest karma (*vāgvijñapti-karma*), and thus only four are mentioned.
Since bodily manifest karma (*kāyavijñapti*) is analogous to vocal karma, its meaning can be inferred accordingly. It does not say "three branches" combined to make seven.
Chapter Seven: On the Superior Meaning of Taking Refuge. Regarding the principle that "the meaning of taking refuge is superior because it is inclusive," this refers to the realization of the truth.

The intention of the Dharma Jewel is that when one speaks of taking refuge and paying homage, one must necessarily possess all three Jewels; yet, while paying homage to the worthy (the Sangha) also brings about its fulfillment, it is not strictly necessary to possess them all [simultaneously].

Regarding the passage, "The 'purification by verified trust' (avetyaprasāda) consists of faith and so forth": the intent of this text is now to establish a refutation, which will be reconciled with the subsequent objection.

The object of refuge and veneration is precisely the object of the purification by verified trust—the Three Jewels—and these are also the Three Jewels themselves; why, then, are they not identified as the same?
For this reason, it is stated that "faith and its activity are distinct."
Section: Regarding "one who practices in accordance with the Dharma": this refers to practicing the cultivation of the wisdom of reflection in accordance with the Dharma of the wisdom of hearing.

What is the difference between this "practicing in accordance with the Dharma" and the second [stage], "listening to the Dharma"? Within the practice of the Dharma, what distinguishes "reflection" from the third [stage], "mental attention"? Answer:
Because the second and third serve as causes, they are able to give rise to the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
In summary, the first three are the causes and the fourth is the fruit; this fruit consists of the three types of wisdom.

Section. First, regarding those whose faculties (*indriya*) are not disciplined: because their faculties are undisciplined, they must take refuge in the vessel for refining the faculties (*indriyaparāvṛtti*).
Section. Regarding that which is not a valid basis of refuge: because that which is taken as a refuge is itself free from fear, one does not further speak of seeking a refuge within it.
If this is so, since the Saṃgha Jewel is also included among those taken as a refuge, would one not seek reliance upon it and thus be free from fear? Answer: It is superior.
The *Mālā-sūtra* states: "It speaks only of taking refuge in the name of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the passage, "Because those prior to the seventh bhūmi are in the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*)," the term "stage of the cause" refers to the explanation of the two types of outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) existence: that of body and speech.
The reason for speaking of the "seven stages" is that their meaning extends to include the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

This is because from the eighth stage upward, there is only the outflow-free, whereas prior to these stages, there is only the outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*). Therefore, the term "seven stages" is said to be inclusive.

Section. Regarding the "single realm-location" (*ekadhātu-sthāna*): according to its actual substance, its essence is exclusively volition (*cetanā*). Therefore, among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it is spoken of as the two types of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), with their substances being explained in combination.
Section: Regarding those with ugly forms, this refers to the foul bodies produced by transformation within the desire realm; they cause terror both in other living beings and in themselves.
Section: Regarding the twelve who receive refuge, this refers to receiving the three refuges from a teacher.

Chapter. Regarding those referred to as "the Great Master and others" among the eleven types of virtuous assemblies: the phrase "the Great Master and others" refers precisely to the assembly of the eleven types of virtuous ones.
Chapter on the Four Kinds of Nutriments.
Regarding the phrase "The previous explanation is not so," etc.: this is called "not so" because the intention of the first master’s interpretation differs from that of the subsequent master;
it does not mean that the previous view is refuted by calling it "not so. The section beginning with "It is not necessary... sets forth the intention of the former.

[Commentary: However, according to various texts, for those whose practice and understanding are superior, the treatise merely states that it "gathers and benefits joy" (*prīti*) and so forth; it does not mention the eight consciousnesses. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "the mental faculty (*manas*) is the volition (*cetanā*) that synthesizes the object": the volition associated with the mental faculty is able to contemplate the object and cause it to be integrated [with the mind].

Because they meet. When the mind meets with volition (*cetanā*), there is existence; this existence enables the object to be the focus of volition, and this volition enables the mind to engage in mental deliberation (*manasikāra*) regarding that object.
Question: What is the distinction between the two modes of activity—the hearing and reflecting (*śruta-cintā*) and that which is reflected upon? Answer:

Volition merely cogitates upon that object, whereas the mental factor (*caitta*) is able to cause the mind to perform its functions and so forth; thus, the two are distinct. Alternatively, here we are specifically taking up the characteristic of the mind itself.

One should consider that volition (*cetanā*) constitutes the substance of food. Why is it necessary to state that "volition causes one to contemplate what one has personally heard and grasped"? The principle [of this explanation] is still not exhaustive;
one should examine that passage in the *Vibhāṣā*.
As for that which can sustain and benefit consciousness, it pervades all eight consciousnesses. Some say it refers only to the three [mental] consciousnesses of oneself. However, the first...

Regarding "increasing" (*āpyāyana*): when the self-consciousness (*manovijñāna*) undergoes transformation and decay, it further employs this increase to universally benefit the other [faculties] and so forth.

Some say that according to the general intent [of the treatise], increase occurs only for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) at the time of transformation and decay, whereby it then benefits the various sense-faculties (*indriya*), rather than from the three [sensory] consciousnesses themselves.

One should consult that treatise to fully understand this. Now, I maintain that this does not refer to growth through augmentation; rather, it is by means of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and so forth that consciousness becomes clear and sharp.
How can it be said that consciousness alone is the basis?

Regarding the chapter on "relying upon skillful means": volition (*cetanā*) serves as the basis; furthermore, the arising of the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā-mūla*) and so forth also constitutes skillful means.

Section. Regarding the phrase "these three kinds [of consciousness] reach a state of intensification through their own substance": they attain intensification by means of the three nutriments (*āhāra*). The term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers generally to all eight [consciousnesses];

some say that this is acceptable. Section. Regarding the phrase "and taking the present as its object": this refers to the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*). Section. Regarding the phrase "because it arises in the future":

this refers to the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*). Section. Regarding the phrase "also taking the past as its object": this refers to both contact and volition, which can both take the past as their object.

Section. Regarding the statement that "this meaning is briefly omitted because it concerns volition associated with agreeable contact (*anukūla-spraṣṭavya*)," it is because contact and volition take the present and future worlds as their objects and are agreeable;
therefore, it says "present and future" and omits mention of the past by way of abbreviation.

Section. That which can serve as the cause for subsequent intensification allows that combined consciousness to arise. Regarding the phrase "the mental faculty (*manas*) that has ceased immediately prior," Section Four states:
"That which is the support of the preceding three is the eighth consciousness. This is because it sustains the faculties and the great elements.
It abides securely by means of such seeds and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "it evolves in dependence upon that": "that" refers to the eighth consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "the consciousness that accumulates karma and afflictions for future existence": this refers to the maturation (vipāka) to be summoned in the future by karma and afflictions.

[This is] consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the passage: "By these four types, each having both general and specific [functions]," etc.: *Saṃskāra* (formative forces) can assist vitality and strength; *sparśa* (contact) increases pleasure, craving, and so forth;
and *cetanā* (volition) assists desire, greed, and so forth, causing the consciousnesses of the faculties and so on to abide securely. This is called the "general and specific. That is to say:

They are able to bring about future fruits and so forth. Furthermore, there are those who possess supernormal powers (abhijñā), such as ascending and descending; this can be understood by reflecting upon it.

In the chapter [on nutriment], in order to make the meaning of "faculty" (indriya) clear, enhanced, and purified, the four nutriments (āhāra) are treated individually; they are called the "basis" because these four names clarify and purify the meaning of "attainment" (prāpti).

Section. This refers to the statement: "Because it undergoes transformation and decay, that which undergoes transformation and decay exists. These four passages correspond respectively to the four nutriments (*āhāra*).

The first statement—that what is subject to transformation and resistance (*pratigha*) is not nutriment—is incorrect; the latter statement—that what undergoes transformation is precisely nutriment—is correct. Therefore, they are summarized together, as within each [pair] there is both what is correct and what is incorrect.

Section. Regarding the four types of existence (*bhava*) and the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*): it is because these four nutriments can each individually nourish and increase vitality, and [the latter two] can nourish the faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Section. Furthermore, regarding "pursuing the three kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*) and so forth": first and second refer to all future food;

if one has not previously obtained it, one pursues it by following its initial signs, namely contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*). This refers to the successive pursuit of the three nutriments. Seeking food is precisely the mental faculty (*manas*).
The arising of joy and pleasure is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). The two aspects of volition (*cetanā*) are difficult to perceive.
Regarding the passage on "the production of karma, afflictions, and the consciousness that leads to future existence": because one seeks the three nutriments as causes, there is karma;
subsequently, the consciousness that leads to future existence arises.

Section. Regarding the phrase "the various formations have consciousness as their cause and condition for abiding": for the most part, the various formations take consciousness as their cause for abiding.
That which pervades these is called "consciousness."

Regarding the statement that "even infants and the like are capable of knowing": although they cannot know the essence, function, or modes of activity of contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), they nevertheless engage in mental deliberation and encounter objects;
because they thus confront the objects of the truths (*satya*), it is said that they are "capable of knowing."
Section. Regarding "daily providing for sustenance and so forth": this refers to the daily support of the body. If it were lacking, the body would immediately become emaciated and impaired.
Section. Regarding "there is no abiding without birth": there is no multitude [of phenomena] that can abide without having been born. Therefore...
The commentary states: "Arising-arising is the characteristic of arising.
Regarding the passage, "Because the conditions have not yet been exhausted, [there is] goodness, etc.": this refers to the goodness that can extinguish arising within prior arising.
It is because of this goodness that sentient beings are able to abide.
Section. Regarding the statement that "one dwells by means of life-force" (*jīvita*), this refers to the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

They have never sought food, nor do they consume it; yet, because there is the difficulty [of explaining their existence], it is said in contrast to them that they dwell in dependence upon life-force.
Section. If this is so, why is it that the place it reaches is so vast and pervasive? This point has not been fully explained. Now, the intention of my supplementary explanation is as follows:
if something is not impaired, it is termed "nourished" (*āpyāyita*); since there are places where it is pervasive and nourishes all things, it is because of this lack of impairment.

Section. Regarding the statement that the faculties (*indriya*) are nourished and developed by what is supported by consciousness (*vijñāna*): Question: Since the faculties possess five kinds of superiority over consciousness, how can it be said that consciousness is able to nourish and develop them?
Answer: This refers to the fact that at the time of hearing sounds or seeing forms, the faculties possess superior power.
Now, based on the fact that consciousness is superior for the purpose of serving as nutriment, it is because the eighth [consciousness] sustains the faculties (*indriya*).

Although the five sense bases (*āyatana*) are fully present, they are not nutriment because their realms of bondage (*dhātu-saṃyoga*) differ; furthermore, if they were untainted (*anāsrava*), they would not be considered nutriment from the perspective of what is tainted (*sāsrava*).
Chapter. Regarding the statement, "However, by the power of the noble ones (ārya), it becomes fit to serve as food":

this means that when the power of the noble meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) take [objects] as food, they take only the three—odor (*gandha*), flavor (*rasa*), and tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*)—as food; they do not take visible form (*rūpa*) as food.
Therefore, this refers to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) serving as food.
Section: There is an interpretation that this is not so regarding "reaching the sphere of non-dharmas" (*dharmāyatana*). This master’s intention is as follows:
when the power of concentration (*samādhi*) of an Ārya transforms fish, rice, and so forth, these serve as the predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*).

At the time when the eighth [consciousness], which is *sāsrava*, undergoes its own transformation into fish, rice, and so forth for the sake of enjoyment, it employs only the actual fragrance, flavor, and so on transformed by its own eighth consciousness; it does not employ those [objects] belonging to the sphere of non-dharmas.
...and so forth, regarding form (*rūpa*). The reason for this is that sentient beings’ three consciousnesses are able to employ the form of the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).

[The text] states: "This is also not so; it is only when reaching the three bases that they are called 'nutriment'. This meaning explains that anything capable of providing sustenance is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*);

it is not necessary for it to be an object of the three consciousnesses to be called nutriment. Among the classes of sentient beings above [the desire realm], edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is predominant. Correctly...
Regarding the time of eating, the three consciousnesses take it as their object. If one were to obtain these three times [past, present, and future], they would not yet constitute food;
this case is likewise difficult to justify logically. Why is this so? That which is transformed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the like belongs to the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*);

how could it serve to sustain sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? Furthermore, there would be the fault of [the food] increasing [defilements]. Moreover, since that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) destroys existence (*bhava*), how could it serve as the condition for food?
The power of meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and so forth is not fixed; therefore, one may take what is superior as inferior food.

Nevertheless, there is ultimately a distinction [between them], which involves no error. Furthermore, to speak according to the actual reality, it is simply by means of that form (*rūpa*) that it serves as its substance.
The eighth consciousness itself transforms the matter that is the fruit of karma and experiences it, as is extensively explained through questions and answers in the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning).
Regarding the passage stating that "that which is outflowing (sāsrava) is comprised within the nature of the wholesome":

this is an admission that prior to the seventh stage, one transforms fish, rice, and so forth, such that they possess practical utility. Since outflowing states still function prior to the seventh stage, the outflowing mind is likewise capable of transformation.
Section. Regarding the passage "If it is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), yet it reaches the contaminated (*sāsrava*) because it causes that [contaminated existence] to diminish": Question:
At the time of eating, does one eat only that which is contaminated and transformed by one's own eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and not the uncontaminated?

If so, how can it be said that one destroys existence (*bhava*)? Answer: Because the uncontaminated serves as a remote condition (*pratyaya*), it ultimately enables sentient beings to finally attain [liberation].
Regarding the section on "severing the outflows" (*āsrava*):
if this meaning were too narrow, it would fail to encompass the *Abhidharma* and those individuals below who have attained detachment from desire;
thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not include those lower ones who have attained detachment.

Section. The answer states that there are two types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) reaching down to the three lower levels of the realm of resources (*rūpadhātu*). "Eye, ear, body, and mind" refers to the four consciousnesses.
Since it says "downward," the consciousness, volition, and contact necessarily follow.

In the chapter [concerning] "Question: Does the lower provide for the upper? Because one contemplates the subtle principle," the character "upper" (上) is erroneous; it should be combined as the character "lower" (下).
In the chapter [concerning] "Regarding the distinct meaning of skillful means," this character "fang" (方) is erroneous; one should consult other editions.
Section: Because the realm does not think upon food, there is that which is sought but not obtained.

Section: Regarding the statement that the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) attains growth through accumulation—these first three clarify that by means of these three as gateways, the seeds of karma or the consciousness-link (*vijñāna-aṅga*) function as the cause for future existence; this is termed "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*).
[The] Chapter [states]: "Because wisdom conforms to and benefits relinquishment (*upekṣā*)," this is to exclude those that do not have universal objects (*sarvālambana*).

[The] Chapter [states]: "However, it refers exclusively to the principle of acting as a productive condition (*janaka-pratyaya*) for dharmas that have not yet arisen," because this nutriment serves as the cause-nutriment (*hetu-āhāra*).

It enables the nourishment of all seeds; for those six consciousnesses and so forth are, by analogy, the superior fruits. This is because present food does not sustain that which has already fallen away, leaked out, or ceased.
The chapter states: "If it exists merely as a conventional designation of phenomena (dharma-prajñapti), there is no further experiencer."
Section. Regarding "the untainted is likewise so": this is because it merely maintains the untainted. Section.

Regarding the first explanation that [this] pervades the six consciousnesses: this is because, through merely hearing the Dharma externally, what initially sustains it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), and what subsequently sustains it is called "pleasure" (*sukha*).

The ten courses of action restrain the branches of form. Regarding the statement that there is textual evidence for [the existence of] "recording the mind" (*jìxīn*) and so forth, these are merely skillful means and not the fundamental aspiration for the Way.
(Chapter on the Sixty-two Views, end of Volume Four).
Section: Regarding the phrase "due to practicing different views and associating differently": having views that differ from those of one's teacher is called "different views";
initiating activities separately from the teacher is called "associating differently."

The chapter on "Views Concerning the Past Eon" (*pūrvānta-kalpa*) refers to the past limit (*pūrvānta*). The chapter on "Views Concerning the Future Eon" (*aparānta-kalpa*) refers to the future limit (*aparānta*).

Some claim that "past" refers to the eon of formation (*vivartakalpa*) and "future" refers to the eon of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*), but this is not so. The *Madhyama Āgama* states that five [views] constitute the past limit and five constitute the future limit;
thus, as the *Āgama* says, "the past eon and the future eon," it is clear that these refer to the past and future limits.
Section. Regarding the phrase "twenty phrases, etc.," this refers to the view that form (*rūpa*) is the self (*ātman*), and so forth.
Section. As for the statement that the *Āgama* sūtras cannot be relied upon entirely, the meaning of this is as follows: these sixty-two views pervade the three realms;
since there is also form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are not the ultimate tenet. Since this sūtra is already a [Mahāyāna]...

[The author] states: "O various schools, one cannot rely entirely upon what is taught in that sūtra. While it may be so regarding the fruits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is not so regarding the fruits of karma (*karman*).
As for the passage stating 'by way of the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior purity,' this refers to pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*), which is another name for dhyāna."

Section. Regarding the second contemplation on birth (*jāti-vipaśyanā*): this refers exclusively to contemplating birth there [in the higher realm], not contemplating death here [in the lower realm]. One should consult the *Śāstra* and the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) for further details. Section.
As for the statement that "if one says [it is so], it contradicts the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)," this refers to the first three [types of vision], excluding the last one.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the fourth [type] is named the divine eye; likewise, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the third is named the divine eye. This is why there is a contradiction.
Chapter: Regarding the "Theory of Permanence" (*śāśvatavāda*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that this theory of permanence is further designated as the "Chapter on Permanence.
As for the phrase "or seeing the Brahmā King establish things according to his will": it refers to seeing that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that Brahmā King are permanent;
or seeing that the mind is impermanent; or seeing that one's own body and various requisites are established by the Brahmā King according to his own will.
"Chapter. "One who is like that patient one. "That" refers to the Brahmā King. "Chapter.
"Or one who dwells in the Brahma-world. This indicates that he was personally present when the Brahma language was heard.

Chapter. Or perhaps it was heard through successive transmission; thus it arose here as a report of what others had said. Or perhaps it was in the Brahma-world that it was likewise heard and reported.

Section: "All are based on meditative concentration" (dhyāna). Question: Since it was heard immediately after the second [life] that the Brahmā King spoke these words, how can they be said to be "based on meditative concentration"?
Answer: In the past, while [the Buddha] was still in the higher realms, the Brahmā King spoke so that he might attain concentration in the human realm.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in considering what was heard prior to that point as being based on concentration. Alternatively, it may be that the present Brahmā King spoke concerning the future; thus, it is also designated as the "prior limit" (pūrvānta).
Section. Regarding "all states prior to the emergence of the mind": this refers to all dharmas, including one's own mind, mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and other phenomena.

Section. Regarding "all dharmas are like myself": these "dharmas" refer to phenomena external to the body; taking one's own body as the example, it is shown that these [external] dharmas likewise do not exist.
Question: Why does one not recollect what occurred prior to the emergence of the mind? Answer: Prior to the emergence of the mind...

"One is in a state of non-cognition (acittaka). How can one recollect anything while in non-cognition? Question: "For what reason does one not recollect the states of having cognition (sacittaka) prior to the period of non-cognition?

Answer: "The limit of the recollection of past lives (pūrvanivāsa) by non-Buddhists (tīrthika) is at most eighty [great aeons]. Since one remains in the state of non-cognition for five hundred aeons, it is impossible to recollect the period prior to that non-cognition.
Question: "Does the recollection of past lives also take form-phenomena (rūpadharma) as its object? While in the state of non-cognition..."

[Question: Although mind and mental factors are unimpeded, material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) still exist. Why do you not take material phenomena as an object and maintain that they are causeless? [Answer:

In all observations of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), one must first observe within the mind before observing material phenomena emerging from the mind. Since the preceding mental factors are already absent, how could one observe material phenomena?
Section. If one seeks the limit of the world by means of the limit of cessation through conditions, this refers to the proponents of the doctrine of destruction (*vināśavādin*).

They designate the exhaustion of the eon as the "limit of cessation. Taking that ultimate limit as the boundary is what is meant by "having a limit" (*antavān*). Because they form such a view and report it, it is called "seeking the limit of the world."

Section: On the Expedient Means for Emerging from Contemplation. "Emergence" refers to the manifestation of the kalpa of formation. "Expedient means" (upāya) is so named because it emerges by means of this [manifestation].
Whether one contemplates the finite or the infinite, the present instance of raising up the kalpas and so forth is likewise an expedient means.

Section. Regarding the three kinds of false conceptualization: although four are enumerated, we now discuss their essential nature; for the fourth is merely the third and thus possesses no separate essence.
Section. First, those who are not pure in goodness are the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Section. Second, those who are pure in goodness are only the Buddhas.
As for those who enter mundane meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their concentration belongs to the non-Buddhists.
Section. Or, regarding "providing a divergent answer": explaining what is wholesome as unwholesome and so forth is called a divergent answer. Section. Or, regarding "denying actual existence":
denying that truly existent phenomena exist and so forth. Some say it should be understood according to motion. Section. Or, regarding "admitting non-existence."
The outsider explains it as follows: When there is a phenomenon (dharma), he asks, "Is this phenomenon not non-existent? He then follows up with questions regarding its being or non-being.

The statement "there is a name for purity" means that there is a name. These three statements together constitute the outsider’s intended response. This provides a comprehensive explanation of the four modes of activity (catur-ākāra).
Section. Furthermore, from the Sage up to the *asaṃpramoṣa* (Non-confused) Heaven, there is one who answers [questions] without confusion; thus it is named the *saṃpramoṣa* (Confused) Heaven.

However, according to the Buddha-dharma, that is not called the *asaṃpramoṣa* Heaven. At first glance, it might seem as though it is so named because of answering without confusion, but since it is named in relation to the questioner, the Buddha-dharma also names it the *asaṃpramoṣa* Heaven. Reflect on this.
"Chapter. Regarding 'according to the location': this refers to whichever region of the world it may be. Chapter.
Regarding 'not yet opened according to the case': this means that although one is in the same Pure Heaven (*śuddhāvāsa*), one has not yet attained liberation."
Section. Although there is a nature that possesses consciousness, although there is a nature of understanding, there is the fundamental statement of following recollection.

Section. Regarding the answer concerning the formation of false views: because the view is not correct, it is termed "false" (邪); this does not necessarily refer to the "false view" (邪見) among the five types of views.

Section: Regarding the failure to respond as constituting false speech. Although he did not explicitly state, "I have the power of testimony," he nonetheless implicitly claimed to possess such testimony.
Now, by failing to answer at all, he who previously asserted that he had testimony is thereby said to have spoken falsely.

Section. Regarding these three types that metaphorically rely upon other matters: "metaphorical reliance" means having a mode of activity identical to those other matters, each of which has its own distinct characteristics;
these are precisely [the afflictions] such as fear of destruction and so forth.
Section. Regarding the statement that the three lower levels of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also pertain to that [category]:

as the Mahāsāṃghika school says, if one asserts that there is indeed form even in the formless realm, then my category of "possessing form" (*rūpin*) would also include the formless. Why, then, are the three lower formless realms excluded [from the category of "having no form"]? Answer:
Because they are not among those who are "neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñin*). Reflect on this.
Chapter Seven. Regarding the seventh chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"The two types of grasping at a self through various perceptions" refers to those in the lower stages—namely, the three heavens below the fourth dhyāna and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The desire realm is easily understood. In the first dhyāna, one perceives the distinctness of joy (*prīti*) and so forth; in the second and third dhyānas, one perceives the great [bliss].
Regarding the calamity of water: because there is a distinction between minds that possess fear and those that do not, as stated in the *Fahua chao* (Excerpts on the Lotus Sūtra), Chapter One:
"I have pure happiness" up to "the three lower dhyānas. This means that in these three [dhyānas], there is exclusively the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
Chapter. Regarding the passage "I have coarse form... up to its cessation": this refers to those in the human realm of the desire world who arise within the evil destinies;
because of the extreme suffering there, they do not bring about cessation. This is as explained in the *Fahua chao*.

Section. Regarding the various devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): they are distinguished separately from the human realm; therefore, they are treated as distinct categories. Section. Regarding the various devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*):
in this section, those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are combined into one. "Formless" (*ārūpya*) is the opposite of "form" (*rūpa*).

Section: On the Indeterminate Nature of Self and Other, up to the Attainment by All. Whether one calculates it in terms of one's own body, or in such-and-such ways regarding the bodies of others and oneself, what is now explained as "extinction" is attained by all. Therefore, it is called indeterminate.
Section: "I have attained mastery over the mind through liberation. This means that because of my liberation, the mind is sovereign. Section:
"Attaining mastery through contemplation" means attaining sovereignty over the objects transformed [by the mind]; this is called attaining mastery through contemplation.
Some say that "attaining mastery over the mind" refers to the two practices of *śamatha* (calm) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), yet they do not clearly explain the reason for this.
Section. This teaching is superior and subtle; it is rarely found among humans, whereas the *Vibhāṣā* states that it exists [there]. This passage is suspected of being erroneous.
Section. "Abiding in fullness" means attaining the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Section. Why are there not two heavens—the Heaven of the Thirty-three and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings? Section. As for the question regarding the destiny of the immortals (*ṛṣi-gati*):
are there those who, having passed away from among the immortals, attain rebirth in heaven, while others do not pass away and thus consider themselves eternal?

For what reason are they not established as a separate category? Answer: These difficult points and extensive details, including the distinctions of the Dharma, are all as explained in the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning).

Regarding the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa), in each chapter: for one who has not yet internally subdued and eliminated the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), their own internal body’s perceptions of beauty and ugliness, as well as craving and so forth, have not yet been exhausted or removed.

Question: Is it the case that by departing from the afflictions of one's own stage and attaining the [liberations] of emptiness, consciousness, and so forth through the six modes of practice, one is immediately designated as having attained the eight [liberations]?
"Is it liberation? He replied: "Some say that being free from the defilements of one's own level is not the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

As for the eight liberations, they require the superior practice of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within the state of liberation. While this may be the case for non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), disciples of the Buddha cultivate liberation solely by relying on the contemplation of the truths (*satya*)."
Section. Regarding "the one who sees" and "the appearance of the established form-phenomenon": "The one who sees" refers to the seer.
For the seer, the observed characteristics of form are established and appear before them. Question: How are the characteristics of form established and made to appear for the seer? Answer:

Some say that although one is free from the defilement of form, there still remains an obstruction to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because one still perceives beauty and ugliness, these characteristics of form are established in accordance with the mind.

Now, as for the commentator’s explanation: because one has already become free from defilement, in order to cause the obstacles to move even further away, one establishes the appearance of the characteristics of form and contemplates them as being present before one.
Section. Regarding the statement, "From the first three liberations (vimokṣa), one induces the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana)," etc.: Question.

Do one cultivate the spheres of mastery only after having attained the eight liberations, or does one induce the spheres of mastery while possessing only a few? Answer. There are two explanations. One says: Having attained two liberations, one induces the first four spheres of mastery;
subsequently, one gives rise to the third liberation, the "pure" (śubha) liberation. Once that liberation has arisen, one induces the [remaining] four spheres of mastery.
Regarding the bases: having first attained the four bases, one subsequently understands and cultivates the remaining liberations (*vimokṣa*).

Second, it is said that once the eight liberations have been definitively attained, one induces the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) as appropriate. For now, let us explain based on the latter [interpretation]. If that were so, then only the second liberation would have been attained.
Regarding the first two *abhibhvāyatana*s (bases of mastery) which are "without internal form," why is it further stated that there is "internal form"? Answer:

It is called "having form" (*rūpī*) because form is established within; it is not called "having form" merely because one has not yet abandoned defilements. As the *Abhidharma* says: "Liberation is called 'creation' (*nirmāṇa*)."

The cultivation of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) is called "arising," while the application (*prayoga*) for the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) constitutes their fulfillment; thus, there is a distinction in the sequence of these three types.

If one were to interpret them as previously explained, the cultivation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality would become confused. Consider this further.

Section. Alternatively, as for those who see [the form] without the perception of form (*arūpa-saṃjñā*) being established before them: because they are beginners in their practice and have not yet attained spontaneity (*anābhoga*), they must establish the formless state before them.
Question: Even if it is not established, what fault would there be in relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) alone to contemplate [the form] as small, large, and so forth?
Answer: Some say that one must first establish the perception of the formless to suppress and eliminate the perception of form in the observer.

The perception (*saṃjñā*) begins by relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) to effect liberation, because that [perception] first eliminates concentration and provides further remote protection. Question:
Neither the *Yogācārabhūmi* nor the *Abhidharma* mentions "few" or "many" and so forth. On what basis is this stated? Answer: Since the second [verse] already says "the rest" (*śeṣa*).
As explained previously, it should be understood in that way. Question: Regarding the first liberation (*vimokṣa*) and so forth, how is it that one performs the meditation on light?
Is it as previously established for the few or the many? Answer: One takes the few or the many objects previously apprehended and establishes them as light;
therefore, there is no fault. Reflect further. Some say: "The perceiver is the ideation of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) established and manifest before one, which has not yet been attained."

Regarding the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*): those who suppress and eliminate [the perception of form] by means of the contemplation of the Truths (*satya-darśana*) rely on the perception of form; or alternatively, they rely on the contemplation of reality (*tattva-darśana*). Question: The first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) contemplate only the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Why, then, is it said only regarding the second liberation that one has "already become detached from desire for form" (*vītarāga rūpāt*)? Answer: In actual fact, they are equal. However, the first [liberation] is established based on the combination of two fruits and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as it involves both joint and solitary practitioners; therefore, it is not yet free from form. As for the second, having already attained the fruit of the Non-Returner (*anāgāmin*), it is called "detachment from form. Furthermore, because the first liberation is based on the contemplation of the loathsome (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), it does not transcend the perception of form. The second liberation, however, relies on the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*), and thus transcends the perception of form. Therefore, it is said that one has already become detached from desire for form. This is the distinction between the two. Moreover, the first liberation is established based on the contemplation of the internal and external, whereas the second liberation is established based solely on the contemplation of the external. It is said: "The disciples of the Buddha attain the fundamental dhyānas solely by relying on the contemplation of the truths (*satya*), not by relying on the six practices as the non-Buddhists do.

For example, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, one may immediately attain the first fruit [of the path]. How could it be said that the six practices are used to attain the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*)? Others say:

Regarding the first interpretation: if both have not yet attained the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they both rely on the contemplation of the truths (*satyadarśana*) to suppress and sever attachment to form.
Furthermore, "not contemplating that perception" means not taking that initial sign of light as a mental object.
Section. Now, regarding this second [case] of "having internal form and having external forms such as those with sense-faculties," this contradicts the [previous] assembly.
Other texts state that "having internal form" means having external forms such as those with sense-faculties.
Section: Regarding "the one with correct knowledge of the world," the cultivation of the sixfold wisdom is also termed "correct knowledge.

Section: As for the statement that "one only attains [the state] upon reaching the preceding path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and then attains liberation (vimukti)," this refers to the process of entering the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), wherein one again performs the path of uninterrupted transition followed by the path of liberation.

Section. This refers to the contemplation of external forms and the contemplation of those possessing form. Regarding "contemplation of external forms," the first part explains the Mahāyāna, while the subsequent section on "those possessing form" and so forth explains the Hīnayāna;
this is because the initial contemplation in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* involves contemplating external forms.

Chapter: On the contemplation of various forms and the contemplation of external forms while being internally formless; this chapter provides a combined explanation and analytical reflection according to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Chapter: Regarding the gate of following the principle through one-sided mental resolve and contemplation of the pure and subtle; this follows the *Abhidharmakośa* of the Hīnayāna.
Thus it is said. "That which is called 'purification' alone is termed a single resolve" (ekābhisamaya).
Regarding the phrase "the states such as concentration and so forth upon which various things depend": these refer to the simultaneous mind and mental factors.

These very concentrations and so forth are designated as the "bases. Concentration and the others are not singular; they are the various supports, which are themselves the qualities that depend [upon them].

Because it is that upon which space depends, it is called the "supported basis" (*āśraya*). Regarding the statement that the objects of focus for the practitioner who is the "supporter" (*āśrita*) are space and so forth:
this cites the supporter in order to reveal the supported. The practitioner who is the supporter refers to qualities (*guṇa*) and the like. Thus one reflects.
Section. Regarding "there is nothing else and no separate object": outside of that which is non-existent, there is no further object. Section.
Regarding "having observed that the objects above are non-existent and minimal": to observe that consciousness is external [to the object] is called "observing what is above. Some say:
The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) takes the infinite as its object. If one is weary of form (*rūpa*) and is reborn there, it is because all [states] therein are formless;
thus, one takes that very space as the object. However, being weary of the activity of form does not necessarily require taking space as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to form.

This is like the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which merely involves being weary of the mind and causing it to cease, yet does not necessarily involve space. Therefore, one is simply weary of form. Question: Does the mind of nothingness (*akiñcanyacitta*) merely involve reflection?
Because there is no other phenomenon outside of the sphere of the base of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), it is called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).

Does this liberation also take as its object the Four Noble Truths of oneself and others, as well as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and other such phenomena? Answer: It takes as its object the Four Noble Truths of oneself and others, and so forth.

However, liberation is subsumed under the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). If one does not understand the distinction between "self" and "other," that too is included within the hindrances; if one does understand it...
Name. It removes one portion of the obstructions. If one wishes to understand name, one must contemplate the consciousness that dwells therein;
as for the objects such as matter and mind external to the precepts, they are without name and without existence. Otherwise, how could it be said that "name" is non-existent?

Even the liberation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) induces this knowledge and speaks of "formlessness" (*ārūpya*). As for "not taking the lower as an object," it means not taking the lower realms as an object. Furthermore, others do not...

That which is capable of effecting liberation cannot take it as an object; thus, it is not universal. Consider this further. Question: To answer this objection, one merely becomes weary of form (*rūpa*) and performs a contemplative resolution (*adhimokṣa*).
Therefore, one takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as objects, and no longer takes the lower stages as objects.

If there is "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*), then one takes the lower consciousness as an object, because within that consciousness there is no such objective sphere as emptiness and so forth; hence it is called "the subtle non-existence. If that is so, then...
What is the difference between this and the station of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*)? Answer: In the station of consciousness, one contemplates only that there is consciousness and nothing else;
thus, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, one gradually enters true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*) and only then severs the obstacle of emptiness.

This explains that by taking True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the object of focus, one first contemplates light and its varying degrees, and only then enters true contemplation to sever the obstacle of meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*). Once the obstacle of concentration is severed and True Suchness is realized...
By means of this contemplation, one attains the realization of the suchness of conditions (*pratyaya-tathatā*). Regarding the term "suchness of conditions," it appears in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
As for the phrase "by way of the characteristic of mutual inclusion," this refers to their reciprocal inclusion of one another.
Section. Regarding the severance of these two obstacles: they are the two [realms] of form and formlessness. Section.

As for the distinction between ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), among the noble ones there is both that which is obtained through the separation from defilement (*vairāgya-lābhika*) and that which is pure;
for ordinary beings, it is exclusively obtained through preparatory effort (*prayoga-lābhika*). One should further examine that text.

Section: Regarding "because one attains mastery by removing the obstacle to transformation," this refers to attaining mastery over the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that arise from the liberations regarding form (*rūpa-vimokṣa*).
This description applies to noble ones (*ārya*); it is not the case for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Section. Regarding the statement that "it is not said that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not perform the first three [meditations]": since the treatise does not state that ordinary beings do not perform them, it is clearly known that ordinary beings are able to perform them.

Section. Regarding the phrase "by this, conversely revealing that [the attainment] reaches [all levels], it thus applies to both internal and external existences": this is the intended meaning. Since the treatise does not say "only... [it implies the opposite].
The Noble Ones attain it; the disciples of the Noble Ones do not. This clearly shows that although they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they nonetheless attain it.

Regarding the phrase "those who are outside," "outside" refers to ordinary beings, or alternatively, "outside" refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). That treatise merely states that they mostly indulge in craving for flavors;
it does not categorically prohibit their attainment, as there is no textual exclusion. One should examine that treatise accordingly.
Section. Regarding the phrase "contrary to the characteristics of pure form up to transformation": it refers to grasping what is pure as impure and clinging to that as being fixed and real;
this obstructs their mutual dependence. Regarding the explanation of "the application of effort for transformation":
it means that regarding the transformation of pure form into impurity, one applies effort but cannot achieve it; or, regarding the "effort," it means applying effort toward pure form.
"Use" (*yòng*) refers to practicing with attachment. Impurity (*aśubha*) is to be understood by analogy. Regarding the subsequent explanation of "good":

the two factors of affliction (*kleśa*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are explained according to the meaning within the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhy-āvaraṇa*). Alternatively, one may hear that they do not exist among the hindrances to meditative concentration.
Section Six: Regarding the "causing that which has reached liberation to become distant. This refers generally to taking what follows as its object; it is the definitive abandonment of hindrances.
One should consult that treatise for further details.
Section. Regarding the statement, "When the time for subsequent fulfillment arrives, one attains the subsequently arising [state]," the intent of this proof applies to both realms.
Since the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the form realm serve as its cause for the attainment of fulfillment, it is clear that there must necessarily be the fruit of liberation.
Just as a beginner requires wisdom as the cause to be able to attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*), once the division [of the practice] is completed, concentration itself becomes [the cause].
Wisdom is the cause and [the fruit] is the result.

Regarding the section stating that "the cultivation of the perception of purity is not limited to the desire realm": the cultivation of purity can also be attained regarding forms within the formless realm. Some say, furthermore, that it refers to the distant cultivation of the perception of purity regarding the visible forms of the desire realm.
As for our current interpretation: even if one were to cultivate the perception of visible forms such as color and so forth belonging to the form realm, what fault would there be?

Question: Regarding the phrase "attained through the separation from desire," does this mean one attains it immediately upon separating from desire, or is it attained by further practicing skillful means? Question:

If it is said that attainment through the separation from defilement refers to what is based on abandonment (*prahāṇa*), why did you previously state that the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) is suppressed and eliminated? Answer: This is in view of...
The meanings are distinct. With respect to abandonment, suppression, entry, and accompaniment, they each have their own distinctions, yet these do not contradict one another.

Now, having attained liberation, when one enters the observation of one’s own object, what kind of mental aspect (*ākāra*) does one employ? Answer: One subsequently employs the previously cultivated aspects of practice, which become even more intensified.

The two interpretations are each distinct. As for the term *siddhi*, there is no corresponding [Sanskrit] equivalent; therefore, it is not translated. However, these four characters merely serve as an auxiliary to the character *sa*, acting as a pseudo-suffix.
Section: Regarding "based on the fundamental self, there is no object": based on the fundamental grasping mind, one falsely conceives of a self and its objects through the attachment to a self;

yet these have no substantial reality. Section: Regarding "therefore, the view of a self in phenomena is likewise produced as the view of a self": this arises in the same manner as the previously explained production of the view of a self.

Chapter: On the Exclusion of Defiled and Pure Intention. That which is obscured [but indeterminate] is subsumed under the categories of defiled and pure, as well as unobscured-indeterminate and wholesome.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: On the Twenty-Seven Noble Ones (Fifth Volume, Part One).

Section: Regarding the statement that "having abandoned six or seven categories [of afflictions], one has half a birth remaining," it is actually the case that having abandoned seven categories, one has half a birth remaining.

As for the mention of "six," this is because by abandoning six, the principle [of the remaining] applies; the seventh category is what remains to be abandoned, and thus the term "six" is used as a designation for half of those six. Consequently, the character "six" is redundant.
Section. Regarding those who have first entered the path of approach (*pratipannaka*): the preceding fifteen moments of mind are termed "approach. Why are they not further mentioned in the text?
One should consult other sections.
Chapter. Regarding the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) and sixteen aspects (*ākāra*): among the sixteen moments of mind, the eight knowledges constitute the essence.
