Since the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) derive from knowledge, they are simply designated as the eight knowledges. Under each of the four truths, there are four types of aspectual modes; these are called the sixteen aspects. Question:

In the preceding fifteen moments of mind, the four aspects of the three truths are all "approaches" (*pratipannaka*). How can they be collectively described as being "fruits" (*phala*)? Answer: Only...

The path-knowledge of the category of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) is the correct cultivation (*sammukhībhāva-bhāvanā*) for the first fruit; as for the remaining seven knowledges, they are acquired through cultivation (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) at the time of the first fruit.

Since the essence [of this stage] consists of both correct cultivation and acquired cultivation, it is said that there are eight knowledges. Regarding the four aspects of the path, these constitute correct cultivation, while the four aspects of each of the three truths constitute acquired cultivation;
these are likewise explained in terms of knowledge. As for why one does not emerge from the second fruit: [this refers to] the second fruit.

Alternatively, it may be a variant reading; thus it is not explained. Or perhaps it is a textual omission. Regarding the third and fourth fruits, one suddenly cultivates the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) and sixteen aspects (*ākāra*);

this is to be understood according to the explanation of the first fruit. Question: Since the delusions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) have already been eliminated by the first fruit, and since those [delusions] are not severed by the third fruit and so forth, why is the eighty-onefold unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) taken as their essence? Answer: Because the fruits are collectively [unconditioned].
This is why there are eighty-one [types of practitioners]. All of these are based on the Hīnayāna; one should verify this in treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Regarding the statement that they "turn toward the first three fruits" and so forth, in truth, these two sets of four fruits each have distinctions between those of sharp and dull faculties.
However, this is established based solely on the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). If all four were established [in this context], it would result in confusion.

Now, as for the statement that the first three fruits are all present, the reasoning is somewhat difficult. Why is this so? If one considers their substantial existence (*dravyasat*), all four fruits exist.
It is not only the first three [stages]. If one considers their establishment, only the first fruit (srotāpanna) does not rely on the middle two; therefore, it is untenable.
One should consult the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, etc.

Section. Regarding those who are "body-witnesses" (kāyasākṣin) within the third fruit, this is stated according to their specific distinction; yet generally speaking, all four [types of practitioners] possess this quality.
Among the Arhats, the sixth type—the Immovable One—is a "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta), while the remaining five are "those resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
Section: On the accomplishment of those antidotes. This refers to accomplishing the three, four, and six antidotes. Section:

Question—Should not the [first] three mentioned above also be included in abandonment? Answer—Regarding this question, the first three grades are abandoned at the very beginning when the wisdom of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arises with sharp intensity;
however, when the Path of Cultivation arises again subsequently, these do not enter into abandonment. Furthermore...

The middle and lower [levels] require three times the effort to become free from desire; therefore, the first [level] is not required. Because the [middle] three are not doubled [in effort], one enters [the path] and immediately abandons them.

Furthermore, because the first three categories are coarse, they are easy to enter; the middle three are subtle, so while they are abandoned, entry is not instantaneous. One should consult the *Abhidharmakośa*;
there is no such text in the Mahāyāna, yet those who interpret it as being consistent with the Mahāyāna do so without error.
Section. Regarding those who reach the body of the first dhyāna and then sever [the fetters] to take birth: this is the "half-leaper" (ardhapluta).

It differs from the "full-leaper" (sakalapluta), who goes directly to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) or the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa); it also differs from the "universal-extinguisher" (sarvasthānacyuta), who takes birth in every stage (bhūmi).

Because this one takes birth according to whichever specific stage [is appropriate], it receives the name "half. Now, these three types depend on the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas); they die in the body of the first dhyāna and are reborn above.
And thus they are established. Therefore, these three types all state that one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn above.
Regarding the response concerning the explanation of the four fruits: the intent of this response is to say that the arhat is spoken of for the sake of establishing the four fruits;
if the arhat did not exist, the four fruits would not be definitive.

Chapter. Answer: Regarding the establishment of six distinct [paths] based on the differences in lineage (*gotra*), one should consult the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts for the distinctions among the three [types of lineages].

Chapter. Question: Why were the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) not included in the preceding [section]? Answer: This refers to the path of seeing as representative; the same applies to including the unconditioned states of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This is because they do not exist in the "candidate" (*pratipannaka*) stage either. Answer: The intention here is that the meaning of "progressing toward" (*pratipanna*) does not apply to the unconditioned.
Therefore, it is not accepted. This has already been explained in the preceding section; hence, no answer is provided here.

Regarding the passage in that sutra stating, "There is no way for one born there to be reborn in the desire realm," this is the response. Both interpretations are included therein. It is certainly not the case that they pass away [from there].
The lower record is erroneous, as it lacks the reason why there is no passing away: because they fear birth and death, they are not reborn above.
Regarding the realms: when the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are exhausted, one is no longer born in the desire realm. For this reason, one certainly does not pass away [there].
As stated in detail in the *Vibhāṣā* (Guǎngzhāng), an error was recorded; the passage concerning "An" is found within the section on questions.
Section. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and many obstacles": because it is a state of negligence (*pramāda*), negligence itself is termed an obstacle, as it is the dwelling place of Brahmā alone.
Section. Regarding the question "To which realm does it belong?": this text contains an error; one should consult the original source.

Section. Regarding the statement: "There are those who possess the fruit but are not yet in the stage of the path (mārga) leading toward it, nor in the stage of non-retrogression (anāgāmin)," this was the intent of the previous question. Now, however, the question is posed by taking into account those who, while possessing the fruit, are also still on the path toward it; it does not take as its starting point those who possess only the fruit or only the path. Since the first fruit and the fourth [fruit] are exclusively fruits and not paths, and the first path is exclusively a path, the present answer—within that context—states:

[The text continues: ...In the case of the first fruit, there are two types: one who has attained the fruit but is not yet in the path, and one who is both in the path and possesses the fruit. As for the fourth fruit, there are likewise two types: one who has attained the fruit but is not yet in the path, and one who is both in the path and possesses the fruit. Therefore, the answer here applies to those who possess the fruit and are also in the path toward it. Thus, it is said: "One who has attained the fruit but is not yet in the path" refers to one who has already realized the fruit but has not yet entered the subsequent path. "One who is both in the path and possesses the fruit" refers to one who is currently practicing the path while simultaneously maintaining the realization of the fruit. This is how the distinction is made. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "nor in the stage of non-retrogression," this refers to the stage where one has definitively severed the defilements and will no longer regress; such a person is neither merely in the path nor merely in the fruit, but has transcended both. This is the meaning of the response. Therefore, the text concludes: "This is the meaning of the answer. This clarifies that the distinction between being in the path and possessing the fruit is established based on whether one is currently engaged in the practice of the path while maintaining the realization of the fruit. This is the definitive explanation. Thus ends the section.
This is the answer. If it were not so, for what reason would one not accept it? One should consult the *Guangzhang* (Extensive Commentary).

Regarding the passage in that chapter which asks, "How does one abandon the eighth category [of afflictions] of the desire realm? etc., seven characters have been omitted here. This is the intended meaning of the question therein.
If eight or nine [fetters] have not been severed and there is still the arising of a fruit of existence, one may be called "Ekābhijñika" (One-Interval).

Since the eighth [fetter] has already been severed and only the ninth remains—being inferior and lacking even half a birth—how can one be called "Ekābhijñika"? The answer is: this meaning is based on the teaching regarding a minor birth, whereby one is named "Ekābhijñika."
There is no contradiction here either.
Regarding the phrase "because the two natures are confused and complex": since the two natures are difficult to distinguish, one does not act and enters parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, regarding "those who weary of birth and death": "birth" refers to nature (*prakṛti*). Because there is only this single nature which is infinitely free from weariness, one attains nirvāṇa. This is the brief [explanation].
The name for "discourse" (yan) signifies that there is no satiety [in its exposition]. This commentary does not provide such an explanation, as the underlying principles are difficult to discern.
Briefly, there are five meanings, as explained in the *Guangzhang* (Extensive Chapter). The *Sanke zhang* (Chapter on the Three Categories).

Section: Regarding the statement that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) pertain to both natures (dvividha-svabhāva). Question: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), Chapter Eight, states that the five aggregates and so forth are subsumed under all three natures (tri-svabhāva).

Now, you speak only of two; does this not constitute a contradiction? Answer: Here, we are discussing the essential nature (tattva) of the aggregates and so forth. Since the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) lacks any substantial reality, it is not mentioned.
The same applies by extension to the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).

Section. Regarding the exclusion of "one" from "the union of self up to the union with consciousness" as a single unit: Question: To hold that "one" is opened into "ten" colors contradicts the principle of this section.
How can the union of consciousness into one serve to dispel the attachment to the union of one? Answer: It is because of the attachment to the physical body as one that the self is opened into ten.
However, when writing of mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), one does not perceive and thus does not attach to them. Since "one" is not separately opened out, it is not [dispelled].

It is not opened; this excludes that single synthesis. This section relies on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to refute the mark of synthesis (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) as a means of discarding conventional designations.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation that "joy in form" and so forth, up to "opening the mind," constitute seven [factors], these texts are erroneous; one should consult the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Section: Regarding the statement that the three—liking, disliking, and so forth—are provisional based on their nature (*dhātu*): the "nature" referred to here is not the nature of essence (*svabhāva-dhātu*), but rather the nature of function (*kāritra-dhātu*).

It is said that because liking, disliking, and so forth do not exist [as independent entities], they are "evil in essence"; yet, because they are able to give rise to the mental states of liking and disliking, they are provisionally designated as "liking" and "disliking.
The substance upon which they depend is real and co-emergent (*sahaja*). Since these two substances are co-emergent, they are not mentioned [separately].
Taste is conventional; its nature is conventional. This should be understood by analogy with odor. This is because the nature of bitter taste is a conceptual designation.
Chapter: Regarding "that which arises from mastery over meditative concentration is real," this means that the matter produced by meditative concentration is real.

Section. Regarding the statement that "the form of the meditative object is provisional": this means that the form which is the object of contemplation through conceptual construction is called the "meditative object.

Section. Regarding the phrase "like the Brahmā King who initiated the debate": this refers to that Brahmā King who did not answer the Brahmā assembly with deceitful words, but instead spoke the words uttered to Aśvajit;
these were all encompassed by concealment (*saṃvṛta*). He raised his hand to welcome Aśvajit, which was a bodily action (*kāyakarman*) characterized by concealment.
When unwholesome or obscured minds do not arise above [the level of the formless realm], it is termed "obscured bodily and vocal intimation" (*avijñapti*); yet in reality, it is not itself obscured.

Chapter Twenty-four: On the Non-associated [Conditioned Phenomena] (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). As for "according to what is appropriate," this clarifies their nature by following that upon which they depend.

Section: Regarding "that which is definitely induced within the dharmas," this refers to the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because it is induced by concentration, it is called "induced by concentration.
Section: Regarding "conceptualization and deportment": when the conceptualizing mind falsely constructs the object as form, it is called "conceptually constructed form" (*parikalpita-rūpa*).
When the conceptualizing mind produces an interpretation of deportment toward the object thus conceptualized, it is called "deportment" (*īryāpatha*).

[Section] Nine. Regarding the phrase "among the five realms of transformation," the character *jie* (界, realm) is an error; it should be combined with the preceding to form the character *yun* (蘊, aggregate).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "only taking the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)," the character *yuan* (緣, condition) is also an error; it should likewise be combined to form the character *yun* (蘊, aggregate), as the eighteen realms are individually distinguished below.

If this is so, how can one now say "only the aggregate of form" when the text below states that within consciousness there is only the sixth [consciousness], and so forth? Answer: This refers to what is transformed.

Because that which is transformed consists solely of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) and so forth are not what is transformed; thus, the sixth [consciousness] is said to be the "transformer.
If this is so, why are the visual and auditory consciousnesses called "capable of transformation"? Answer: The two types, visual and auditory, are not actually transformers.
However, because the two [bases, i.e., the eyes and ears] possess the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are designated as "transformation."

Section. Regarding the "wholeness of the five objects": some say that according to actual reality, all transformed [phenomena] are subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects); however, when speaking of the five objects in relation to the sense faculties, they are designated as the five sensory domains. Section.

Regarding the "four objects that support the faculties" (*indriyopakaraka*) which do not arise from karmic retribution: these are each subsumed under their own respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

This section states that there is no separate, intrinsic nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) apart from the maturation-indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*). This means that, apart from the maturation-indeterminate, there is no other distinct entity possessing an intrinsic nature that is indeterminate.
Since the category of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) is broad, it subsumes those [other types of indeterminate phenomena].

Chapter: Regarding the analysis of conditions based on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is according to the *Sthiramati-ṭīkā* that this refers to the analysis of conditions by way of the immediately preceding [moment].

As for the statement in the *Paramāṇu-varga* (Chapter on the Atom) and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "it reaches the point of total extinction in the interim," yet further states that it does not [reach], this clarifies that there is no real atom (*paramāṇu*). If...
There is a real subtle [particle]; it should be called "arrival" (zhì).
In this chapter, the explanation of "arriving at the subtle" and "arriving at the limit" (biānjiè) does not mean that the limit is named after reaching the edge of the ultimate atom (paramāṇu).
Rather, the space occupied by seven ultimate atoms is designated as the "limit."

Regarding the passage beginning with "one is then able to purely and extensively cultivate," it means that because one’s faculties and all forms and minds are free from even a single thought of attachment,
one is thus able to extensively cultivate pure conduct.
Section on the Five Advantages: First, because it takes the two kinds of emptiness as its expedient means; second, because it further leads to the discernment that penetrates form;

third, because it can sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; fourth, because it subdues arrogance; and fifth, because it removes the entanglements of afflictions and all [conceptual] marks.

Section. Regarding "practicing various contemplations on emptiness until reaching the ultimate subtle atom": this means that when one wishes to practice the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one must first break down form and so forth.

Section. Regarding "because one subsequently enters into emptiness": the character "subsequently" (*hou*) is an error; it should be "attained" (*de*). This is because one attains emptiness by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, in this chapter, the distinction between the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) and the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is made: that which acts as a cause is named origination, while that which acts as an effect is named suffering.
Unlike the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), where the essence and meaning of these two truths are divided differently, here the two are definitively distinct.
Record of the Determination of the *Fayuan yilin zhang* (Treatise on the Forest of Meanings in the Garden of the Dharma), Volume Lower Part I.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhizhou.

Regarding the chapter on the matter-form that is the fruit of supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*): "The mind abides and functions of its own accord" means that it arises by means of a mind of mastery. "Arises" has the sense of "producing.
"Chapter" refers to the subtle nature; this speaks of how this matter-form of concentration is subtle.

Section: Regarding the measure of space and the locus of earth. Space is the measure of a single hair-tip; earth is the measure of a single particle of form. Taken together, these constitute the measure of space and earth.

[The] Chapter [asks]: "Is it that even those of the Two Vehicles and so forth cannot undergo transformation? According to the *Xiányáng shèngjiào lùn* (Exposition of the Holy Teachings), even the noble ones of the Two Vehicles cannot undergo transformation.
[The] Chapter [states]: "Because it is permitted for the gods of the Formless Realm to shed tears," which cites the aforementioned Āgama to prove that ordinary beings [can do so].
It is a transformation. Question: Since it only mentions rain from the heavens and does not speak of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), how can we know that ordinary persons can also give rise to it?

Answer: Since it only mentions rain from the heavens and does not state that it belongs exclusively to the noble ones (*ārya*), it does not obstruct ordinary persons; therefore, it applies universally.
This section clarifies that it is not the object of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*). It states that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is called supramundane wisdom;

it does not include subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If this were not the case, for what reason would it be said that it is not the object of supramundane meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?

Section. Regarding "the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the form that is the fruit of the superior meditative concentration one practices": this refers to the resolute conviction regarding the form that is the superior fruit resulting from such practice.
For this reason, everything is accomplished exactly as it is. This phrase marks the conclusion of the main thesis within the text.
Section. Regarding the explanation of the first *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery): this refers to the first among the eight *abhibhvāyatanas*. Section.

As for the phrase "if one who is superior [perceives] the objects of form that are subsumed [therein]," it means that in the practice of these *abhibhvāyatanas*, there are characteristics of knowledge regarding qualities such as superiority and inferiority.
Now, the general meaning of "equal and superior" is cited to verify this. Since one relies on the *abhibhvāyatanas* to contemplate sounds, fragrances, and so forth, they constitute the eight.

One also contemplates liberation in this way. Subsequently, one arouses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to transform the objects. Although liberation and the like are the causes, they likewise transform the five sense objects.

As for the statement that "because the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) prior to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is inferior, it cannot produce transformations," that refers to the fact that the preparatory practice prior to that absorption only transforms—
The three realms of form do not transform into odor or taste. The reason for this is that those states of meditative concentration lack odor and taste;
furthermore, the preparatory mind does not intend to transform them. Thus, the preparatory mind itself is designated as the cause.
Section. Furthermore, even if one transforms them such that they lack actual utility, [one might ask]: "If those transformed colors and so forth also lack actual utility, why transform them at all?
Answer: Although they lack actual utility, because these three exist within this meditative stage (*samāpatti-bhūmi*), they can be transformed.
"Without using incense and so forth.
This section [addresses the objection] that one cannot say [the sense organs are unnecessary] because they have practical utility; this is a restatement of the opponent's challenge. Reflect upon it.
"The sense organs serve as the support for consciousness... because they possess the five objects. These are all explanations of the challenge. It can be understood by reflecting upon them.

Regarding the statement that what resembles the sense organs (indriya) is comprised solely within the five [objects] such as form (rūpa), this is because they lack the functional capacity of a sense organ and are therefore subsumed under the five sensory domains (viṣaya).

As for the passage: "However, from the condition of that [object], up until its manifestation," it means that once the great elements (mahābhūta) have undergone a transformation to produce an image based on the object of touch, the great elements of the meditative concentration (samādhi) then transform to create this coarse condition. Furthermore, these must necessarily be produced by the great elements of form and touch.
Section. Regarding the phrase "the first, the karma of the sense-base of tangibility," etc.: the term "etc. includes the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*). Section.

Regarding the phrase "this is exclusively the result of meditative concentration" (*samādhiniyataphalam eva manas*): the four characters "this is exclusively the result of meditative concentration" (*samādhiniyataphalam eva*) are superfluous; verify this against other editions.

Section. Regarding "or the objects of the five consciousnesses": the matter produced by meditative fruition (*samāpatti-phala-rūpa*) pervades and transforms the five sense-objects; therefore, it is the object-condition for the five consciousnesses.

Section. Regarding "or it is pervasive and non-tied": since it is admitted that the untainted (*anāsrava*) can pervade all eighteen realms, and because it contacts the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is pervasive and non-tied.

Section: Regarding the preceding cause of meditative concentration. Prior to concentration, the initial mind first transforms the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and subsequently produces derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Thus, this preceding mind is designated as the "cause."

Section: Regarding this "the Great Pervasive One creates the realm of the three consciousnesses," the eighth, the sixth, and the five consciousnesses are taken as one; these are called the "three consciousnesses. Section:

It is also admitted that the power of meditative concentration first gives rise to the fruit of concentration. That which arises as the fruit of concentration is the "matter of the fruit of concentration" (*samādhiphala-rūpa*). This refers to the fundamental...
Regarding the phrase "because consciousness and so forth arise from derived matter which follows the great elements": the term "and so forth" includes the five or six consciousnesses.

This means that because those [consciousnesses] are determined by form, the objects of the eighth [consciousness] and others likewise take as their objects derived matter transformed from the great elements themselves.
Section. Regarding the statement that "this text says [it is so] because it is produced later": according to the first passage, this refers to the sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).

It explains that once the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) bound by meditative concentration have arisen, derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is subsequently produced; only then can that derived matter, by virtue of being bound by those [elements], be designated as "matter of superior concentration" (*samādhiviśeṣarūpa*).
Section: "Although fixed, they also transform" refers to those produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

This means that when the fixed four primary elements transform their own immediate capacity to produce fixed derivative matter (*rūpa*), they must rely upon the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) as the objective basis (*bimba*); only then do the primary elements of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-mahābhūta*) transform to produce fixed matter.
Now, speaking from the perspective of the objective basis, it is said that [the former] is the initial producer.

Section. Regarding the statement that the primary elements (mahābhūta) of meditative concentration are not said to be the basis for its arising: it is because the four great primary elements of the meditative state do not belong to the body itself.
Rather, it is said that the matter which is the fruit of concentration arises directly dependent upon the primary elements of contact (spraṣṭavya).

[The] Chapter [states]: "However, it is not that the primary great elements (mahābhūta) themselves directly produce [the derived matter]. Here, "primary great elements" refers to the essential substance of the tangible objects. [The] Chapter [further states]:

"According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, this applies up to 'not within meditative concentration'. Based on this, the statement that "it is not produced from actual great elements" means that it is not directly produced by the tangible great elements;
thus it is called "not produced from actual [elements]. This does not mean that the great elements do not directly produce [matter] within meditative concentration.
The name is not necessarily produced [simultaneously].
Chapter: Regarding the phrase "if the primary elements (mahābhūta) are not directly productive," the names of the three consciousnesses follow the previous principle;
they should be considered "productive" in relation to the resultant derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) by way of dependence, but this is not direct production.

Section. If, regarding the subsequent "great elements" (mahābhūta) reaching up to those that are not remote, the great elements of the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana-mahābhūta) are the direct producers of the resultant form (vipākaja-rūpa) at the same time.
Section. If, regarding the initial production up to the "uncontaminated" (anāsrava) producers, it is designated as such in terms of the great elements and in terms of remote dependence.
It is created. As for why that which is below can create that which is above, this can be understood by reflection.
Regarding the section [on] "or when one's own location can create another location," there are two explanations. The first says: it is just as the Sūtra states:

Contemplate how the ear-faculty enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and emerges from the faculty-gate samādhi, such that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the ear-faculty produce the form-fruit (*rūpa-phala*) within the eye-base gate.
Second, it is said: contemplate how the great elements of this touch-base arise as the transformation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Regarding the phrase "the matter of the meditative absorption of another's body," this does not reach the level of the first explanation.

As for the statement in the treatise, "this depends on the great elements (mahābhūta) that constitute the basis," this initial passage refers to the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) produced based upon the great elements that constitute the physical basis.

Section. As for the passage beginning with "If, based on this point, one asks: 'Is it not the case that there are no great elements (mahābhūta) [producing derived matter]?'—at the time of entering meditative absorption, one does not rely on the tangible object as the substantial basis.
Furthermore, the preparatory mind prior to that absorption does not form the intention: 'First transform the great elements, and afterwards transform the derived matter.
Nevertheless, within that absorption, the fruition of the absorption arises. How could this matter that is the fruition of the absorption lack the great elements as its producers?"
The section states: "That which follows its respective basis up to the third locus" refers to the emergence of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Whenever one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there are various bases such as beds and seats; therefore, the great primary elements of these objects serve to create the form that is the fruit of the meditative state.

This differs from the preceding two; therefore, it is called the third. It is not only the bed and seat that are designated as the third; rather, the term "both" indicates that the two preceding [factors] which act as the creators are all subsumed within the third.

Section. Regarding "only observing the place": this is the initial preparatory means (*upāya*), which serves merely as the basis for initiating the mind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) and does not give rise to the matter of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rūpa*).

If it were otherwise, since the meaning of the preparatory means would be identical [to the others], why would there be three? [If they were identical,] one would simply be unable to initiate [the practice]. Now, the supporting argument states:
because the preparatory means is the very beginning, the mind is sharp and intense; the other three are not the beginning, and thus they do not serve as a precedent.

Furthermore, since one can attain the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the initial preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), how could it be accepted that the preparatory stages do not give rise to the Path of Seeing?

[The *Śāstra*] states: "Moreover, excluding the intermediate [heavens]. This interpretation is unsatisfactory because it follows a specific context. The reason for this is that there is a scriptural teaching stating that when Brahmā came to the Buddha’s presence to hear the Dharma, he approached as far as the boundary of his own realm;

the Buddha then spoke to him... [self-... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Abhidharma, likely the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*. The translation reflects the technical terminology of the genre.)*
It must not be that the original arising mind causes the transformed matter of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rūpa*) to become its own support before it can be attained.
For this reason, one should know that this [position] is also untenable.

As for the statement in the *Śāstra* (Chapter) that "the untainted (*anāsrava*) is not discussed," this is because the untainted is not bound (*abandhana*) and thus cannot be discussed in terms of the distinctions of the three realms.
The names are not to be discussed. Question: Since that which is transformed by the Tathāgata is also exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), why is it said to pervade the three realms?
Answer: From the perspective of the ultimate nature, this is a matter of the Buddha’s manifestations; thus, there is no contradiction.

Section. Regarding the wholesome and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Question: Is this fruit of meditative concentration now concentrated (*samāhita*) or distracted (*vikṣipta*)? Answer: If it were concentrated, why would it be called indeterminate?
For concentration is exclusively wholesome. If it were not concentrated, then as something subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it could not be called distracted.
This is also described as *samāhita* (composed). Answer: This matter is extremely difficult. The meaning is transmitted through tradition, yet the explanations are not entirely complete.
It is neither entirely concentrated nor entirely distracted; for this reason, it receives the names *samāhita* and *avyākṛta* (neutral).

It is like when one first awakens from sleep but has not yet fully woken: it is not called a state of total consciousness, yet it is not called a state of total sleep. This case is likewise. Reflect upon this.
Section. Furthermore, because a bodhisattva is exclusively virtuous, even their play is for the sake of benefiting others; therefore, it is solely virtuous. Section.

As for the claim that "the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) arises spontaneously," this refers to that which arises from the mind’s intention within concentration and is immediately negated;
it is not like the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which require the subsequent application of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) before they can be transformed.

Section. Regarding that which is either the transformation of the fundamental [consciousness] or its fruit: it is definitely the fundamental [consciousness] when it is universal, and it is the fruit when it is restricted. Because it is a restricted fruit.
Section. That which arises through the power of concentration on the fundamental object is the object of perception for the fundamental [consciousness].

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if it is the object of liberation, etc.," "universal" (*sāmānya*) refers to liberation itself; "the object transformed by the universal" refers to the object observed by liberation. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "yet the universal can induce both the faculty and the object," because the universal encompasses both superior meditative concentration and inferior states, it is termed a "universal faculty."
The Chapter on the Ten Causes (end of Volume Five).
Regarding the term "conformative cause" (*anuvāda-hetu*): the expression "conformative statement" (*anuvāda*) alone would be a *tatpuruṣa* compound;
however, the term "conformative cause" (*anuvāda-hetu*) is a *karmadhāraya*. Here, the word "cause" is stated in its general sense.
Section. If one waits for the subject that receives (*pratigrahaka*) in order for there to be an object received (*grāhya*), [one might ask: what is the difference from the previous case? Answer:

In the former, that which is received comes first; in the latter, the subject that receives comes first. Although the priority of before and after differs, the object received is of one kind and applies to all cases.
Section. Regarding "because there is that which is common to others," this refers to what is received; it is so called because it can receive others. Section.

If one were to categorize them according to remote conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*), then according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, specifically the section on Vitarka and Vicāra, with the exception of its seeds, it is the cause.
The "appropriation of seeds" is subsumed under the "cause of arising.

As stated in the eighth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, regarding the phrase "based on the superior and middling," this refers to the superior grade; however, the middling and superior grades do not induce the inferior grade.
Section. Regarding the statement that "the subsequent realm is narrow while its nature is broad": it is called "narrow" because it only induces [karmic results] within its own realm;
it is called "broad" because it encompasses both wholesome and unwholesome natures, thereby summoning vipāka (maturation).
Section: Regarding the statement that "the various defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) and pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) are contradictory," they are not contradictory.

It is because of the defilements that they are contradictory; this is said by way of combining the causes. As for the term "application" (*prayoga*): it clarifies the preceding causes based on matters such as arising (*utpāda*).
Once those matters have been completed, these two [causes] are further explained based on arising and abiding (*sthiti*); therefore, they are termed "application."
Section: Regarding the statement that there are both *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional) explanations—this means it is not only a *tatpuruṣa*, but can also be a *karmadhāraya*;
this can be understood through reflection.

Section: If the essence of the cause for conventional designation (*prajñapti-hetu*) of "purity" pervades all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), then one might speak of the untainted (*anāsrava*) with an unwholesome mind.
Dharma. That is to say, unwholesomeness serves as the cause for purification. The rest may be understood by analogy. To speak generally:
if one examines [the stages] up to the nature of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*) comprises the six bases (*ṣad-āśraya*).

The *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderfully observing wisdom) acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the defiled seventh consciousness; the seventh consciousness is the fruit, and the observing wisdom is the cause. Based on this:

Regarding the limits of meaning (*artha-pakṣa*), the fruit can thus be categorized as either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or belonging to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). For now, I have cited the manas; the others should be understood by analogy.

As for the statement in the treatise that "it also reaches the three natures even in its superior grade" (*viśiṣṭa-prakāra*), although this explanation has been offered, the reasoning is somewhat difficult.

When comparing the contaminated three natures to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), the uncontaminated may indeed be called "superior. This is because there is a distinction between the contaminated and the uncontaminated, and [the uncontaminated] is wholesome (*kuśala*).
[Objection: Since there are distinctions such as between the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and so forth, how can they be called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*)?

Therefore, [your position] is untenable. [Response: Chapter: If it is argued that the specific difference among pure phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) persists until the fruit—which is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—then this is said in terms of the ultimate.
To explain the intended meaning of the ultimate: all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena serve as causes for the uncontaminated; thus, they are all factors that act as causes for the unconditioned.

Section. Regarding the statement, "If one can equally discern [them] as penetrating through to the three natures": this means that from the perspective of relative dependence (*apekṣā*) up to the perspective of differentiation (*viśeṣa*), these are all termed "identical in function.

Thus, the subtle contemplation (*sūkṣma-darśana*) and so forth serve as the equal and immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the seventh consciousness; this is termed "discerning manas" (*manas-viniścaya*).
This is also similar to the inclusion of the meaning [of the term].
Section. If one speaks of this in general, what prevents it from also applying to the three natures? To answer specifically, [the unwholesome and the obscured] do not apply;
however, when speaking of them collectively, they may indeed apply to all three.

Section: The Explanatory Causes of Defiled Phenomena. Question: Since defiled phenomena have already been subsumed under the three natures of the out-flowing (sāsrava) category below, why are ten indeterminate (avyākṛta) causes explained here?
Answer: The meaning of "defiled" is broad, whereas the meaning of "indeterminate" has specific distinctions; therefore, they are explained separately.

Section: Regarding the distinctions between cause and effect, etc., although both are sensations (*vedanā*), they are distinguished according to their causal relationship; thus, that which is capable of being felt depends upon that which is felt.

As for "the distinctions should be contemplated," this refers to how painful sensation depends upon pleasant sensation, and so forth; although they are collectively termed "sensation," there are distinctions such as suffering and pleasure.

Section. If one relies on manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) regarding the principle, what fault would there be? If considered from the perspective of manifestation, what prevents cause and fruit from both being common [to all three natures]?
The phrase "the head of the wholesome and so forth" cites its manifest form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the phrase "there is a small portion of the causal basis for defiled attraction (*saṃkleśa-ākṣepa-hetu*)," the intended meaning here is as follows:

with respect to the aspect of karmic attraction, there exists a small portion of the substantial entity of the causal basis for defiled attraction that can be distinguished from its nature as a result (*phala-bhāva*). This is not the case for all [aspects]; therefore, it is said to be "only a small portion."

Section. If the appropriation of affliction reaches the point where its dharmatā is identical to that of the former [purity], then just as the cause of the appropriation of purity is exclusively pure, the fruit of this appropriation would likewise be exclusively afflicted.

Section: Regarding the statement that "the nature of the induced result is the same as the former," it is similar to its inclusion [in the previous category]; this can be understood through reflection. Section: It may also be that this explanation is not necessary.

This is because when explaining the causes of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it is stated that they are all capable of serving as the causes for their respective superior results of the three natures.
The treatise states: "Because they serve as the cause for the superior. If one does not accept this now, it is because it is not based on the three natures.
That which is to be attained should serve as the cause; however, because the treatise deals only with the category of superior causes, it does not mention those of a different category.

Chapter: If one considers whether the contaminated wholesome [states] extend to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) by way of their causal nature, "contaminated wholesome" refers to the six paths of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

If these six paths of action are capable of severing afflictions (*kleśa*), what prevents the causes and effects of defilement from also applying to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Question: In the Mahāyāna, the six paths of action do not achieve [severance];
although they are bound, they only achieve non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). How then can it be said here that they realize dissociation (*visamyoga*)? Answer:

Although it is true that the six paths of action themselves do not realize dissociation, because they serve as the cause by which one subsequently attains the realization, it is spoken of in this way based on a remote [causal] relationship. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]...
This section discusses the Sarvāstivāda school. According to them, one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) through the six paths [of action]. Nevertheless, that school does not assert ten causes.

In the passage stating, "From 'definite difference' (*niyata-viśeṣa*) up to 'the substance pervades both wholesome and unwholesome natures,' the characters 'fruit' (*phala*) and 'dharma' (*dharma*) have been erroneously transposed."
It should be stated again as "if it were conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). The character "if" (*ji*) is redundant; one should consult other editions.

Regarding the passage from "the cause of contradictory characteristics" to "exclusively of a wholesome nature" (*kevalakuśaladharma*): Question: Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) serve as the support for all dharmas.
How can it be said that this is the contradictory cause of the dharmas of affliction (*saṃkleśa*)? Answer:

Once True Suchness (*tathatā*) has been realized by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), the afflictions are then severed. Based on this aspect of the meaning, that True Suchness is said to be the contradictory cause. Otherwise, it would be somewhat difficult [to explain]. Question:
Since the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is contradictory to the state of an Ārya, why is there no affliction therein? It should be inferred according to the purity of its cause.
This is the answer. It is stated here that what is not obtained [as a result] is precisely the cause for defilement (*saṃkleśa*).

The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the opposite of the noble state (*ārya*), but it is not the cause that is the opposite of defilement. Purity (*vyavadāna*) should be understood by analogy. Question:

If that is so, why does the explanation of the etymology state that "the opposite is itself the cause"? Answer: The previous statement that "it is itself the cause" was not made with reference to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but was spoken as a general description.
That which can be described is the cause (*hetu*). Now, in terms of its nature (*svabhāva*), it differs from the contradictory cause (*viruddha-hetu*) chapter.

Regarding the statement that "the fruit (*phala*) is the seed (*bīja*) and pervades all": while the cause is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), it may pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*);

the fruit, however, pervades all—contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth—because everything that is obstructed is designated as a fruit. Therefore, it is so named.
"Kuan" (寬) also [applies]. The remainder may be understood by analogy. Chapter:
"In reality, there are no indeterminate [dharmas] on the fruit. This means that in reality, there are no indeterminate [dharmas] upon the Buddha.
Chapter: "For the sake of ultimate establishment. This refers to being ultimately established as wholesome.
The section on "pervading both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)" explains the synthesis of cause and effect.
The section on "manifesting form by depending on water and so forth" states that the form manifested within water is the color of a reflected image (*pratibimba-rūpa*).

Regarding the passage, "Taking the external barley and so forth as the eight appropriations," this is the explanation of the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*). In the treatise (*śāstra*), based on conventional designation (*prajñapti*), it speaks of external barley and so forth;

however, in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the cause resides in the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state of the seed. Just as the seeds of names and words (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-bīja*) are also indeterminate, they constitute the very cause.
Section Four: Regarding the six distinct categories concerning the establishment and abolition [of dharmas], they have been explained in detail and with brevity in the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning).
Section Five:
Regarding the "Chapter on the Five Fruits," the term "general" (*zong*) refers to the general discussion of the five fruits as a whole.

Section. Regarding the phrase "based on the general" (*sāmānyam āśritya*) therein: because those particular dharmas fundamentally depend upon the general, it is said that by depending on the general, they obtain the designation of "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*). Section.

Regarding the phrase "that which is abided in by the six practices," the character "abided" (*zhu*) is an error; it should properly be "obtained" (*de*). This is because [the path] functions to sever the afflictions.
Because it attains dissociation (*visamyoga*), it is subsumed under the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Regarding the phrase "that which is superior is called 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*)": this excludes that which is not superior but merely brings about [a result].

Regarding the passage "the multitude of fruits only achieves the present; there are no five fruits": the word "only" (*wei*) is likely a scribal error. The intended meaning is that although the fruits are numerous, [they are all included therein].
The essential nature [of the fruit] should consist of only five [results].

Regarding the passage, "This relies on the holy teachings up to the point where it applies to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)," there is no textual passage in the Mahāyāna holy teachings that states the unconditioned can obtain the two fruits of *adhipati* and *puruṣakāra*. If one follows the Hīnayāna, however, I do indeed allow for its acquisition.
Section: Regarding the neutral (*avyākṛta*) in relation to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, this explains the cessation of maturation (*vipāka*).
Section: To clarify that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) results in one or two fruits—first, the unconditioned fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga*);
second, the conditioned fruit of dominance (*adhipati*). Maturation is distinguished according to its characteristics.

The section on the transformation of matter within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is presented here in five parts; this is according to the *Abhidharma*. This chapter is fundamentally based upon the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.

First, regarding "reflected images" (*pratibimba*): they arise either by depending on a substantial basis (*upādāya*) from which they are transformed, or they are manifestations that appear upon one's own mind.
Section Two: Accomplishment of What Is Done. This refers to the fact that the fruit of meditative concentration possesses practical utility. Section Three: The Invisible.
This matter of the fruit of concentration is "matter of the seven locations" (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*). It is called "matter" because it is not visible to the eye.

If this is so, how is it that ordinary beings in this realm see the body of a Buddha, Brahmā, and so forth? Answer: As for the statement that they "are able to see," this occurs through the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of another's concentration.

Because it is cited [as a source], it is not mentioned here. To speak according to its essential nature, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth, is not fixed.
Master Cei says: "The matter (*rūpa*) of meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and so forth, is not seen by the eye.

When citing this text as proof while claiming that one sees it, it is merely for the sake of the dependent origination of the world; it refers to the fact that objective matter arises from conditions.

Section. Regarding "not produced from actual primary elements": this matter is not produced from distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*), but rather arises either from the primary elements that serve as its support, or from the primary elements of the material object itself.
Section. Regarding the sixth point, "belonging to the mental characteristics": this section generally belongs to the evolving consciousness (*pariṇāma-citta*).

Section. Regarding the seventh point, "the mundane" (*laukika*): it is for this reason that it is called "mundane. It is stated that while [the previous discussion] universally addressed the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), here we distinguish only the contaminated;
furthermore, it is said that "the mundane" refers to the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*), thereby distinguishing the causal capacity.
Section: Regarding the objects of one's own and others' stages. The transformed matter of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rūpa*) is common to both self and others as objects of perception.
Because Brahmā kings and others transform their own bases for their own enjoyment, it is called "one's own object. Because they induce others to see it, it is called "another's object."

Section: On the seeds perfumed as causes giving rise to subsequent sense-bases and objects. Because the seeds are perfumed by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone through its own characteristics and objects, these seeds act as causes to subsequently give rise to sense-bases and objects.
If this were not the case, then seeds would be produced by the solitary, distracted mind alone;

for when the mental consciousness operates with the five [sensory] consciousnesses as conditions, it does not take those bases as its objects. Furthermore, since the mind acts as the cause, it is not said that it takes them as its objects—like the hair of a tortoise.
The pervasive conceptualization arising from a rabbit’s horn perfumes seeds, which subsequently give rise to actualization. The Commentary states:
"To take the cause according to the fruit" means that the name of the root from which something arises is designated as its fruit.

Section: On the Shadow Following the Substance. It is said that pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita) consists of images which exist in dependence upon their objective substance (*ālambana-vastu*).

Question: Things such as flowers in the sky or the hair of a tortoise are pervasive conceptualized forms (*rūpa*); since they cannot produce any result, they cannot be categorized by way of their result. To what category do they belong?
It is not subsumed under intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, it is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Answer: This is said to be subsumed under the fruit (*phala*).

Since it is of the same seed as the view (*dṛṣṭi*) and arises as a manifestation of phenomena (*dharma*), it is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) accordingly; therefore, it cannot be said to exist within the sphere of mental objects.

Section. Regarding the statement that "whether provisional or real, it differs from other categories," this discussion clarifies the specific intent behind distinguishing the twelve [factors] of the meditative fruit (*samāpatti-phala*) from the remaining four within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), or the specific intent behind distinguishing them from other sense organs, objects, and so forth.
Some say that the phrase "in all their distinctions" belongs to the following section, specifically within the context of establishing only the three types and so on.
Section. It stands to reason that the *dharmāyatana* consists of only three types; the author of this treatise has briefly distinguished them and established them as three. Section.
Regarding the statement concerning the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth, how is it so here? One may understand this by reflecting upon the critique of the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*.
Section. Shadow and darkness. This reverses the preceding light and radiance.

Section. Regarding the distinction between the upper and lower views up to the "manifestation as one with space": those who observe from above are called "space-as-one" (ākāśaikya), while those who observe from below are called "directed toward" (abhimukha).

Section. Regarding the six kinds of form subsumed under the element of form (*dhātu-rūpa*): "element" refers to the form of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu-rūpa*). It consists of light, darkness, shadow, glare, and the single expanse of empty space. Section.
Regarding the five sense organs and five sense objects transformed within the causal state: this omits one character; they are those transformed by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The faculties are all subsumed within the category of parikalpita (the imagined).

Regarding the passage on "the objects of concentration, such as form," the term "concentration" (*samādhi*) here refers to the concentration of the distracted mind; that is, it is *samāhita* (equipoise).

If it were *samāpatti* (meditative absorption), it would be included within the fifth mastery (*vaśitā*). Why, then, is it said to be included within the parikalpita? [Because] seeing it otherwise would be useless.
The phrase "and so forth" indicates that these [mental factors] necessarily arise in relation to those sense organs and their objects. Some say:

"Excluding the state of outflow-free (anāsrava) cognition, all pervasive mental images within the causal stage that lack practical utility are collectively termed 'pervasive' (*vyāpya*); this refers to the substance of this form. This interpretation is incorrect.

For below, it is admitted that there are conventional forms (*prajñaptirūpa*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If all conventional things were subsumed under "conceptual construction" (*parikalpita*), what other conventional phenomena would remain within meditative concentration?
Is this a case of metaphorical usage? Chapter:
First, regarding the general meaning: it is a brief synthesis that aggregates various forms and summarizes them. Chapter:
Regarding the phrase "this form" up to "predominance as the identity of the holder": the term "form itself" (i.e., *rūpa*) serves to distinguish it from "pervasive form" (*vyāpya-rūpa*). That...

Regarding the phrase "Because it pervades matter, the *karmadhāraya* [compound] is superior," the commentary states: "Since 'matter' (*rūpa*) is already a pervasive name, the first interpretation is superior. Now, since the intention here is to clarify that it is the extreme limit of matter, the first analysis is a *karmadhāraya*:

the extreme limit itself is matter; matter exists at the extreme limit. As for the second analysis: it is the extreme limit of the turning-away from matter; it is the "isolated matter" (*prādeśika-rūpa*).
This refers to the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). The ultimate limit of "distant form" (*prāntakoṭika-rūpa*) belongs only to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Because the sphere of phenomena primarily maintains distant form and does not encompass [all] discourse regarding it, it is considered inferior. Among the three explanations, the "ultimate limit of the distant" refers to the discourse on the ultimate limit within the sphere of form; therefore, it is superior.

Section. Regarding "pervasive color" (*prabhāsvara-rūpa*): it is called "pervasive" because it subsumes both light and shadow within that pervasiveness; thus it receives this general designation. Section.
Regarding "the location being vast and furthermore capable of serving as a basis": "vastness of location" has the same meaning as "pervasiveness. Light and so forth exist based upon pervasive color.
[The] Chapter [states]: "Fearing it would be confused with space" means fearing it would be confused with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) space. [The] Chapter [continues]:
"Furthermore, although the color of distance (dūrasaṃjñaka-rūpa) extends to [space], it is merely called 'extreme distance' (atyanta-dūra). This is an answer by way of analogy.

For example, if one takes the color of distance as the space-element (ākāśadhātu), according to the previous explanation of the term, it is simply called "distance" and not "extending to space"; thus it is named "extreme space. Now...
The same applies to *atyanta-pratibhāsa* (extreme distance). Although it penetrates space, it is not called "extreme emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnya*) simply because it penetrates space;
for this reason, it is designated only as "extreme-distance form" (*atyanta-pratibhāsa-rūpa*).

Regarding the statement that the two names, "dispersed" (*vikiṛṇa*) and "combined" (*samasta*), constitute two interpretations: "dispersed" is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, while "combined" is explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. This is what is meant.
Regarding the two explanations: some say that, according to this, the combined explanation should be exclusively *tatpuruṣa* (dependent), meaning "the matter induced by feeling" and so forth.
However, upon examining the combined explanation now, it is actually *karmadhāraya* (appositional); the *tatpuruṣa* interpretation is simply untenable.

Section. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the *prātimokṣa* up to [the *asaṃvara*] is also called "induced by undertaking" (*samādāna-ākṣepa*): this is because it follows the mind or does not follow the mind.
Some say it is because it is the cause of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). To claim that it is designated based on its distinct conditions is untenable.
What is the difference between this and the explanation below?

Regarding the phrase "also, also, two explanations": these also constitute two interpretations by means of both the *karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound) and the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound). This [first] dispersed [interpretation] is the *karmadhāraya*, while the combined [interpretation] is the *tatpuruṣa*.
[Commentary: "Just like a transformation" means that this matter which is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) is like a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*). [Commentary:

"That fruit" means that this matter which is the fruit of meditative concentration is the fruit of the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) preceding that concentration; because one first intends to transform it through the preparatory stage and only then does the transformation occur. [Commentary:
"That object" means that the matter which is the fruit of meditative concentration is the objective sphere traversed by that concentration.

Section: Regarding the statement that "the spheres of liberation and the spheres of mastery ultimately have no practical utility," this refers to the manifestation of many forms and so forth within the mind of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-citta*).
It is by means of these conceptual marks (*nimitta*) that one is able to give rise to unimpeded movement everywhere.
Section: Regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s wisdom is fully capable of manifesting all reflections," this means that even the Buddhas possess provisional images.

For example, regarding all images derived from such things as the hair of a tortoise, or the "self" (*ātman*) as grasped by non-Buddhists—if the Buddha did not take these as objects, he would not be called "Omniscient.
If he does take them as objects, then those images are real. How could such types of images possibly arise from the hair of a tortoise?
[If it were] manifest, then one would know it is merely provisional.
Chapter: Now, as for the phrase "because the Sage has reached the ultimate excellence," this means that he causes others to perceive him as having a physical form;

this is what is called "attaining reality" (*siddhatva*). It is "ultimate excellence" in this sense, not because he causes others to experience [sensory objects], which is why it is called excellence.
Section. Regarding why the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks only very briefly and does not explain [this point]: at the beginning of this assembly, the *Yogācārabhūmi* is cited;
that text states only that the color of the meditative power (*vīrya*) is a real color (*dravyarūpa*), and thus it is omitted here, as the others are merely conceptualizations (*parikalpita*).

Section. Regarding the statement that "from the three grades of mind, up to the latter, these are real matter": when the lower and middle grades arise, and the shadow-form arises as the superior grade, it is called "ripened matter" (*paripakva-rūpa*).
The former is the reflected image (*pratibimba*), and the latter is the ripened state.

Chapter. Question: If the object of cognition and the essence of the cognizing subject are indeed separate, then since the five consciousnesses take their objects based on the primary essence (bimba), and the cognizing subject is already separated from that primary essence, how can there be "knowledge within conjunction" (saṃyukta-jñāna)? Answer: This refers to knowledge within conjunction with respect to the image-part (nimitta-bhāga).

The eight consciousnesses are all comprised within "cognition through conjunction" (*saṃyukta-jñāna*). If one were to call that which is separated from the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) "cognition through separation" (*viprakṛṣṭa-jñāna*), then since both the consciousness and its object are separated [from one another], both positions would be fallacious. If you claim that cognition is "through conjunction" when the object is in close proximity to the consciousness, [then...]
Since both are said to be "separated," how can there be any intimacy? One should seek a sound explanation for this.

Regarding the passage from "all non-real forms" to "up to being useless": this refers to all objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) such as those of a tortoise’s hair, which arise from the same seed as the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that perceives them.
Section. Or that which arises from the same species as its material cause (*upādāna*) refers to atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth.
Section. That which arises from a distinct seed refers to the truly existent matter (*dravyasat-rūpa*) that is necessarily a fruit.

Section. Regarding these two principles, they correspond to the three preceding [sections]; alternatively, there are the two principles of the provisional and the real concerning the functional utility of matter (*rūpa-kriyā*).

Section. Regarding the statement in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* that "distant objects of cognition (*viprakṛṣṭālambana*) and so forth [exist]," this treatise states: "All distant objects of cognition possess an essential nature (*svabhāva*). Section.

Regarding the statement in the treatise that "there are fifteen atoms (*paramāṇu*)," these are the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), plus the [four] forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The results are the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Because their retribution through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is identical, they are combined into five. One should consult that treatise. Chapter:

Next, regarding "the shadow and the extreme clarity (*prabhāsvara*) have no distinct locations," this refers to the division of the upper and lower parts of the matter (*rūpa*) belonging to the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) upon which the extreme clarity depends.

This constitutes the fault of [the shadow] being a transgression and [the sky] being a single manifest color. Since there is no distinction of location between matter and non-matter, one cannot apprehend non-matter.

[This refers to] the realm (*dhātu*). Section. Now, regarding "the distinct images of that kind arising from conditions": this refers to the kind of matter belonging to the dhyāna-realm (*rūpadhātu*). Section.
Regarding "it is said that those are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*") [it means]: the dhyāna-matter produced is created precisely by the primary elements of the kind of matter.
Regarding the statement that "the former takes the essence [of phenomena] as its essence, up to taking name-and-teaching (*nāma-dharma*) as its essence":
"the former" refers to what was previously explained—that whether there is an essence or no essence, all are collectively taken to have name-and-teaching as their essence.
Section: On the position that the aspect (*ākāra*) of consciousness must necessarily have a real substrate (*vastu*). This means to say:

if the substrate is the object-condition (*ālambana*), the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is the aspect; if the image-part is the object-condition, the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is the aspect; [and] if there is only the reflected image (*pratibimba*).

How is it that the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is called the "mode of activity" (ākāra)? If there were only the substantial entity (vastu), how could the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) be called the mode of activity?
Since it is stated that both the subjective and objective aspects are collectively termed the mode of activity, they must both consist of the substantial entity and its reflection. Reflect upon this.
Section. Regarding the statement that "the causes of various forms are termed 'instruction' (nāma-dharma)":

if the fundamental substance is as previously described, then whether one takes various forms as the object of cognition or breaks down various forms, and further takes instruction as the substance, all possess a fundamental substance, just as explained by the former master.
Section. Regarding the phrase "at the end of the kalpa, they are eternally *jia* (假)": the character *jia* is an error; it should be combined with the preceding to form the character *yin* (隱).

This refers to the calculation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who maintain that at the time of the destruction of the kalpa, parents remain eternally subtle; each disperses and becomes hidden, yet they do not diminish or cease to exist.

Section. Regarding the statement that the aspect of activity extends to all minds: if it were only the aspect of activity that constitutes seeing, who would say that all minds and mental factors take their respective aspects as their aspect of activity?
Section. Regarding the statement, "Because the correct wisdom takes suchness as its object and acts as one," this refers to the stage of the practice of vision (*darśana-bhāga*).
Section. Regarding the statement, "If the wisdom that takes suchness as its object reaches the point where true suchness exists":

if fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) also possesses an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), and since this objective aspect is separated [from the subject], toward what else could it be said to directly realize (*sākṣāt-karoti*) suchness? Since it does not directly realize it, which wisdom would then possess suchness?

Section. Furthermore, regarding the question of what constitutes the objective basis (*vastu*) for the various bodhisattvas: this passage intends to demonstrate that although the state [of meditative concentration] possesses the appearance of deportment (*īryāpatha*), it lacks an objective basis.

This clarifies that appearances do not necessarily possess a real substrate. Thus, once these bodhisattvas have completed their preliminary application (*prayoga*) prior to meditative absorption and have entered the state of concentration, they manifest various bodies throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions and preach various dharmas, acting as Buddhas.

[This concerns] the matter. Because of this preparatory application (*prayoga*), after entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), one is able to accomplish various things according to one's wishes.

[The text says: "If it were not so, then regarding the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*). If it were not as previously stated, then since those on the stages above the eighth are constantly in meditative absorption and lack the binding arousal of a separate preparatory application for concentration, how could they enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in every moment? Since it is already admitted that they do so in every moment...

He is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). It is clearly understood that this does not require relying on the sixth mode of deportment (*iryāpatha*), nor does it arise solely from a mind fixed in a specific mode of deportment.

Furthermore, when the sūtra says "entering moment by moment," it speaks of the Bodhisattva’s capacity to do so; it does not mean that he is constantly in the absorption of cessation at every single moment.
If he were constantly in the absorption of cessation, how could all the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth existing throughout a single *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* not have been severed?

This is somewhat difficult; consider it carefully. The eighth [consciousness] takes the sixth consciousness’s *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) as its substantial essence (*ālambanapratyaya*) and apprehends it.

Regarding the passage: "Furthermore, do the Brahmā-kings and others take meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) as their substantial essence?"—the meaning of this is that at the moment when the transforming consciousness (*nirmāṇavijñāna*) that was able to manifest [the body] has ceased during the actual hearing of the Dharma, and since the consciousnesses of meditative concentration and so forth do not manifest at all times, these two shadows [of the physical body and the mental image] exist within this physical form.
Since the image has no substantial essence, upon what could it depend to exist? Since it does indeed exist, it is clear that it is not a mere reflection;
rather, all [images] arise depending upon a substance. Reflect further on this.

Section. Regarding the statement that "the nature-realm does not follow the mind," such as the single mental factor of *dharmāyatana-rūpa* (form within the sphere of mental objects) and other nature-realms—to which category of object (*viṣaya*) do these belong?
As stated in the first fascicle of the *Yideng* (Lamp of Meaning).
The Chapter on the Three Jewels (Volume Six, Part Two).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "reaching all Three Jewels," these are both glosses from that treatise; the intended meaning can be understood [therein].

Section. Regarding the statement that Ananta’s intention is the same as Vasubandhu’s: it is the same as the word "all" (*sarva*) found in the verse of homage at the beginning of Master Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Section. Regarding the phrase "the assemblies and the assembly of noble ones": this is also from the text of the verse of homage in the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* (or *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*).
Section: Those Who Dwell in the Path. Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are called "those who dwell in the path.

Pratyekabuddhas are likewise called "those who dwell in the path" because, among the pratyekabuddhas, there are no [practitioners] of the three preceding fruits or their approaches; therefore, they are termed "those who dwell in the path."
Section. Regarding the phrase "by means of the power of exposition and manifestation": the skillful explanation of all phenomena is called "exposition" (*vyākaraṇa*);
the arising of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is called "manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*).
Section. According to that sūtra, up to the phrase "called the path of livelihood," it distinguishes between the two [types of paths] based on the observance of precepts.

Subsequently, to explain the Dharma of the Noble Path and so forth to others is called the "path of showing" (darśana-mārga). Merely observing the precepts and so forth, without explaining the Dharma of the Noble Path and so forth to others, is called the "path of livelihood" (ājīva-mārga).
Regarding the statement "endowed with six limbs," this refers to what follows: "the conduct is pure," and so forth.
This is suchness; this is the exposition of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the phrase "in the midst of the sweat-path" and so forth: because there is no [attainment of] the first three [dhyānas], one should seek those who possess vision within the midst of the sweat-path and serve them.
Section. Regarding "even unto abandoning": this refers to the teacher. One who possesses the fragrance of the white dharma (śukladharma) is one who possesses the seeds of precepts;
if the seeds of the precepts are severed, it is simply that the seeds of abandonment remain.
"Chapter. One whose faculties are tranquil" is a name for a bodhisattva, because they are able to pacify the faults of the various faculties. "Chapter.

That which is cultivated by those who are noble by reason of their cause," etc.: those who are noble within the causal stage are called "noble by reason of their cause. This is because practitioners of the two benefits (self and others) take only the untainted, true Triple Gem as their object.

Section Two: Regarding the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) as the Jewel of the Dharma. Question: What is the distinction between the Jewel of the Buddha as a fruit and the Jewel of the Dharma as a fruit? Answer:
The fruit of Buddhahood encompasses all phenomena comprised within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), as well as that which is conventionally designated based upon them.

The Jewel of the Dharma, however, refers only to the ultimate truth (*tattva*) that serves as the basis, as well as the various untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena that depend upon it. Thus, there is a distinction between the two.
Section: Regarding those who possess the virtue and meaning of being "dependent. On the basis (āśraya) upon which the Path relies, there exists this dependent [quality].
