The stages of Buddhahood and the Sangha also take these stages; both are termed "Buddha" and "Sangha."

Section. Regarding the statement that "the rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddhas of the celestial realm are likewise": these rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddhas, though appearing alone within the celestial realms, constitute a category of the Saṃgha because they lack the monastic community of renunciants.
Thus, they may collectively be designated as the Saṃgha. Although their practical harmony lacks the formal presence of a community, they are free from dispute in principle;
in this regard, they are similar to bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is said that they are "likewise. Reflect upon this.

Section. Regarding the statement "as in the two realms up to the four fruits": the term "two fruits" refers specifically to the first two fruits; the term "four fruits" speaks of all four types collectively.
This is because the six heavens of the desire realm possess four modes of existence (*bhava*), and thus they are treated as a whole. Now, to provide an auxiliary explanation:

Regarding "the second is as before" and "the fourth": the fourth refers to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). By mentioning the first two fruits, the fruits of those in training (*śaikṣa*) are revealed.
Only the fourth is explicitly stated, while the third is implied by its shadow. Otherwise, why would it be necessary to mention both the second and the fourth?

Section: On the Differences Regarding the Sarvāstivāda School’s Assertion that [the Buddha and Saṃgha] Arise from Merit and Demerit. The Sarvāstivādins state that the conventional person (*pudgala*) composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is neither the Buddha nor the Saṃgha;
rather, they take those untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas belonging to him as the essence (*svabhāva*) of the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

The intention of that school is that both the Buddha’s and the Saṃgha’s five aggregates are tainted (*sāsrava*), and it is precisely these five aggregates that serve as the basis for the untainted dharmas. Therefore, [harming or benefiting them] constitutes [offense or merit].
At that time, their offenses and merits are established.
Regarding the passage "first receiving the refuges, those who take all three vehicles": this refers to the recipient of the precepts universally taking all three vehicles as their refuge.

Furthermore, the statement "from the stage of seeing the path (darśanamārga) upward, even up to the eight [liberations], it is likewise," etc., clarifies the objects of refuge. Sound... [text fragment].
There are five types of *śrāvaka*, three types of *pratyekabuddha*—as explained in the chapter on "Vehicles"—and eight types of *bodhisattva*, which can be fully understood by consulting the text.

Regarding the statement in the chapter, "Distinguishing the real through the means of expression": this means that when one employs expressions to point toward reality, "the real" refers to *tathatā* (suchness). Reality is not the Four Noble Truths, for it is that which is expressed;
since reality is not itself the expression, [it is distinct from them].

Section: Regarding "relying on the expression to manifest the meaning," this means relying upon verbal expressions to clarify the intended meaning. The Three Jewels as a single essence are subsumed under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Section:

Regarding "according to what follows, the Three Jewels as maintained [in the world] are also subsumed under Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*)," this is an explanation that refutes [the previous position].

"Chapter. Regarding "the dharmas of the sound-sphere (śabda-āyatana) and the dharma-sphere (dharma-āyatana)": these refer to the sound-sphere and the dharma-sphere. As for the "five aggregates (pañca-skandha)": the aggregates of sound and so forth exist simultaneously with the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha);

the mind-king (citta-rāja) and mental factors (caitta) are subsumed within the [remaining] four aggregates. Since there is no fruit of principle (li-guo) among the dharmas that sustain [phenomena], this merely clarifies the practice of the teaching (jiao-xing).
Section: Regarding the equal awakening to the dharmas of the three aggregates—namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. Section:
As for the term "non-awakening" (*abodha*), it is asked: Is it because it does not awaken by itself nor awaken others that it is called non-awakening?
Section: Regarding "from many discussions. "Many" means numerous. It is based on the meaning of "many" that the name "Saṃgha" (the Sangha) is established;
it does not necessarily refer to the number of characters written at the end of a discourse.
Section: Regarding the statement, "If the matter of discussing the Dharma arises, does one announce it oneself?"—the meaning of this is as follows:

The Vinaya states that four people constitute a *saṃgha* for the purpose of discussing matters of the Dharma; thus, it speaks of "four people. Those who acquire the name of *saṃgha* are actually three people, while the one who is able to make the announcement is not part of the *saṃgha*.
This is not [strictly] the discussion of Dharma matters; rather, even with only three people present, they may be designated as a *saṃgha*. Furthermore...

It is like the case of receiving [the precepts] from four people: although the legal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed by one person and the reception is undertaken by four, the remaining two do not constitute a *saṃgha* for the performance of monastic affairs.
For this reason, it is known that the three persons who are in harmony constitute the essence of a *saṃgha*.
Section: Distinguishing the Matter of the Dharma. That which is not the substance of the concordant body refers to the individual matter of the presiding *karmavācanā* itself;
the three persons [required] are not subsumed within the substance of the concordant *saṃgha*.
Section: Regarding "that which is realized is no different," it means that there is no distinction between the dharmas realized by the teacher and the disciple.
Section: Regarding "the cause and fruit of that which realizes," the disciple is the cause and the teacher is the fruit.
Section. Regarding the "six kinds of persons" and so forth: the one who can believe and that which is believed together constitute six kinds.
Although the Dharma Jewel, which is the object of belief, is not itself a person, it is also designated by the term "person" because it is realized by persons.

Section: Regarding the abandonment of the objects of focus, karma, and so forth that constitute the suffering of afflictions, it is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) that is capable of abandoning them. One should understand what is to be abandoned.

As for the principle of the teaching—that the object under investigation does not function as an object of focus—it means that one does not take afflictions themselves as the object of focus. Reflect upon this.

Regarding the phrase, "One should recollect [the Buddha] by means of other characteristics," the intended meaning is this: that which possesses the characteristics of the Buddha Jewel is not the Dharma Jewel;
the same applies to the Saṃgha Jewel.

Section. Regarding the statement "the capacity to awaken and that which is awakened," etc.: this True Suchness (*tathatā*) principle is discussed such that its nature as the capacity to awaken is designated as the Buddha Jewel;
its nature as that which is awakened is subsumed within the Dharma Jewel; and its nature as awakening according to one's capacity is designated as the Sangha Jewel.

[The] Chapter [states]: "To distinguish them from those followers, one simply says 'the Sangha,' which would then indiscriminately include non-Buddhists. Now, by saying 'the Buddha and the Sangha,' one excludes the non-Buddhists.

[The] Chapter [continues]: "'The Buddha' refers to that which is easily damaged; 'up to' includes those who have attained the two vehicles. This means that while the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) is easily damaged, what is now being discussed—the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*)—applies universally.

Regarding the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*): if it is said that the teaching of the *dharmakāya* constitutes a transgression (*ānantarya*), this is not known by those of the two vehicles; therefore, it is not taught to them.

As for the chapter on "transforming according to the species" where even [killing] becomes a transgression: for those of the animal species and so forth, even killing does not constitute a transgression;
however, if a bodhisattva belongs to the same class as those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*), killing constitutes the crime of a transgression.

Section. Why are there not three divisions of the "not-arriving"? What is meant by the threefold division of the single part of the principle of "equality of nature" (*samāna-dharmatā*)? When investigating the ultimate intent, it relies upon the seeking of equality;

regarding the fruit, it is also divided into three parts. At the time of investigating the ultimate intent, it is simply a single fruit; however, based on the skillful means of the mind, it is divided so as to attain fulfillment.
One attains the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This is best explained in reference to those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).
Regarding the passage: "Or, although jewels are precious, [one may take] one part of a supreme jewel," this means that even a jewel can be called a "single jewel.
Within the Three Jewels (*triratna*) of the three vehicles, each individual jewel of the three vehicles contains all three vehicles; thus, it is termed a "single jewel."

Second, because the Buddha Jewel (buddharatna) universally applies to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), there are three vehicles within a single Buddha Jewel; the Dharma and Sangha Jewels are likewise so.
Although this explanation is offered, it does not resolve the objection. How so? The One Vehicle Three Jewels possess only one portion [of each], yet they constitute the Three Jewels.
Why? Because the One Jewel comprises the Three Vehicles; that is, within the Jewel itself there are the Three Vehicles. Therefore, it is called the "One Jewel Three Vehicles."

Those who understand it attain it by means of this division. Nevertheless, because it is established as the One Vehicle (ekayāna), one part is established wherein there are the Three Jewels (triratna).
Within the Jewels, there is no scripture; only one Jewel is established. The Jewels do not differ from the Vehicles.
Section. Regarding the phrase "The Sangha is fundamentally not many," etc.: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is precisely the fundamental basis upon which the Sangha relies. Section.
Regarding the statement "Because the Buddha is not of the Two Vehicles, there is no three-in-one": this meaning is explained as follows. One must not say that the Śrāvakas and others are the Buddha;
therefore, among the Two Vehicles, one does not separately establish the existence of the three bodies, but rather [speaks of] only one body.

Section. For what reason are six added to the recollection [of the Three Jewels], making three? One recollects the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; the six are added by including generosity, ethical discipline, and the devas.
Recollecting the three causes one to draw near [to them]; recollecting the six causes one to practice and advance.

Regarding the phrase "having already divided the two types of death" in the Chapter on Destroying Māra: although these are not explicitly listed among the enumerated names, the aggregates of death pertaining to the events of *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) death are nonetheless present.
Section. The evil Māra Pāpīyān is called "The Pair-Raiser. *Māra* is the title; *Pāpīyān* is the name.
The term "evil" (*āśubha*) mentioned above is a designation in contrast to "good" (*kuśala*); it is not a designation for Māra itself.
Section. Regarding the phrase "The divine light is pure; its name is 'sovereign,' and it is called 'heaven'": this passage contains an error in the text.
It should read: "Sovereign and pure light; its divine function is named heaven. This has been verified against other editions.

Section. Or, when the "death-contact" (*maraṇa-sparśa*) simultaneously contacts the vital points (*marmāṇi*), the death-contact itself constitutes the vital points. Its substance consists of the four great elements;
contact with them results in immediate death.

Section. Regarding the two stages of "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*)—namely, the state of being about to die and the state of dying—this is also similar to that [previous] category of "dividing" (*prādeśika*).

Section. As for the statement that only the aggregates (*skandha*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) are designated as the demonic armies: this means that these ten demons consist of the aggregates of affliction.
Hunger, thirst, desire, and so forth are termed "aggregates," while the categories such as the three poisons are subsumed under "afflictions."

Section. Regarding the passage "The heavens and the world [are like] the worn-out [garments of] Ānanda; his mind is equal [to them]," etc., this explains why only three [types of Māras] are established and why the celestial Māra (deva-māra) is not included.
This is clarified by citing specific instances.
Section. Regarding the establishment of "one māra" based on sentient beings: "sentient beings" refers to those possessed of feeling. Section.

Regarding why only the category of karma is not established as a māra: both *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) and *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence) possess afflictions within their karma.

However, when viewed in relation to cause and fruit, its essence is inferior; therefore, it is not established [as a māra]. There is no doubt that transformative karma constitutes a matter of activity.

Section. Regarding the first point, "the categories of sentient beings as provisional or real": the *tathāgata-māra* of the segmented realm (*pariccheda*) is subsumed under real sentient beings; the *tathāgata-māra* of the transformative realm (*pariṇāma*) is subsumed under provisional sentient beings. Section.

Regarding the phrase "because the category of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) [is addressed] last, the latter four are taught": this does not establish the category of afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive hindrances.
Regarding the aggregates, devas, Māras, and so forth, only the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) are established as Māra.

This is because those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) give rise to the inversions of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so on, which obstruct the four virtues of Great Nirvāṇa—permanence, bliss, and the rest—and are therefore also called Māra.

However, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) cannot separately induce distinct ripened results (*vipākaphala*). Thus, it is said that for the two vehicles, the arising of these obstructions refers to the four inversions in relation to Nirvāṇa.
Regarding the character *pan* (槃), there is a textual error here; it should read "obstructing the stage of the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*. Alternatively, it should read "obstructing the four virtues.
In terms of the characters, *nirvāṇa* should indeed be [associated with] the character for "virtue" (*de*).

Section: Regarding the similarity of distinct obstacles. Within both the [two] and the [four], there are both aggregates (*skandha*) and death; thus, they are called "similar" because they are either six or four. Section:

Regarding the statement that "by means of wisdom one realizes the truth, and only then is it extinguished. This refers to the fact that the four knowledges—such as "my births are exhausted," and so forth—are only established through this realization.

Section. Furthermore, regarding "possessing both types of destruction": this refers to the simultaneous destruction of both the fourfold [obstacles] of the *pariccheda* (segmented) and the fourfold of the *pariṇāma* (transformative).

Section. Regarding the statement that Amitābha Buddha has Māras and so forth: this explains the reason for the existence of celestial Māras (*devaputra-māra*) within the transformative [realm], which applies to all ranks above those already named, including the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
It further states: "If one abides as a Bodhisattva," which generally includes those abiding in the ten stages.
Bodhisattva: Now, consider the meaning of the text. It states that dwelling in the seventh stage is called "abiding. Reflect upon this.

In the chapter on the Three Wisdoms (end of Volume Six), there is a teacher who says that these three [wisdoms] reach the seventh or eighth consciousness. This master’s intention is to say that the fruit, the eighth [consciousness], takes [them] as its object.

Regarding the teachings and principles, it therefore encompasses all three types of wisdom. The seventh [consciousness] is likewise; even in its untainted state during the stage of the cause, the seventh consciousness can take the teachings and principles as its object.
Thus, [the claim that it does not do so] is incorrect.
[Commentary]: If it is possible to lead the mind (*manas*) to that which is acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), the latter master restates this previous position, saying:

"It should also be able to lead [the mind] to that which arises exclusively concomitant with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-sahaja*). The latter master raises an example to challenge the former master. [The text continues]: "If that were so, it would contradict the Sacred Teaching.

The latter master restates the former's argument to demonstrate its contradiction with the Teaching; this can be understood through reflection. [Commentary]: "Only when one directly hears the sound is it called..."

Regarding the phrase "the one who hears": the latter master cites the former master. The intention of the former master is that only when one personally hears the sounds of names, meanings, and the teachings of the Dharma does the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) arise.
Since the five consciousnesses do not directly perceive those [objects], they are not the wisdom of hearing.

As for the statement "then the wisdom of the mind (*manas-prajñā*) should also not be [the wisdom of hearing]," this is the latter master’s objection to the former master. The intention of the former master is that at the moment the mental consciousness suddenly hears a sound...
When reflection has not yet arisen, there is no seeking; it is only after seeking that this wisdom arises. Once this wisdom has ceased, one does not directly hear the sound;
thus, like the five consciousnesses, it would not be called "wisdom of hearing. Since the sound is absent at the time of seeking, it is said: "If one hears..."

Regarding the statement, "Sound reaching the fifth [consciousness] should also exist": the latter master cites the precedent established by the former master to establish his own position. The former master’s intention is as follows:
although the subsequent wisdom does not hear sound directly, it is induced and perfected through the mind hearing sound; thus, this wisdom is termed "hearing."

The later masters generally state: "The five consciousnesses are likewise. Although they do not directly hear the teachings on names and meanings, because the sixth consciousness—possessing the wisdom of hearing—induces and establishes the 'hearing' within the five [consciousnesses], what fault is there in this? Therefore, the interpretation of the later masters is correct.

Section. Therefore, that which is simultaneous with ear-consciousness is also "hearing-wisdom" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Even if it is clearly manifest at the same time as ear-consciousness, the mental faculty (*manas*) may also be considered "hearing.
As for the statement that the mental faculty is distinct, the character "distinct" (*bie*) must be an error; it should properly be the character "consciousness" (*shi*). Question:

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "hearing" refers to inference (*anumāna*). Since the mental faculty associated with the ear is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it be considered "hearing"? Answer: The *Yogācāra*...
Furthermore, to clarify according to my own view: this general explanation is somewhat difficult in terms of its underlying logic.

The section stating, "From this, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) extends even to the five sensory consciousnesses," means that while the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the wisdom derived from hearing belongs exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is nevertheless said to extend to the five sensory consciousnesses by virtue of what it induces and so forth.
This is just as the intrinsic nature of the afflictions of conceptualization belongs to the mind, yet it is also designated as such based on the aspect of what the mind induces.

Regarding the passage "It penetrates the five consciousnesses; it does not coexist with the seven consciousnesses because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is profound": although its mode of activity is profound in the untainted state (*anāsrava*), this is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*);
furthermore, it can be understood that there is no volition (*cetanā*) associated with the tainted [state].

Section. Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s wisdom of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) does not coexist with the eighth consciousness: although the aspect (*ākāra*) of the untainted eighth consciousness is profound, there is no non-conceptualization in the state of Buddhahood;
therefore, it can be known that the eighth [consciousness] is not tainted (*sāsrava*).

Section. Regarding the statement that "the term 'contemplation' (cintā) refers to the mental factor of volition (cetanā) according to the *paropagata* (dependent) analysis": the *paropagata* analysis takes the name of the other [member] exclusively.

Now, to say that the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is called *paropagata* implies taking both the self and the other; thus, there is a logical confusion. What is the difference between the *paropagata* and the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) analyses?
For this reason, it is known that the second explanation—that it is a *tatpuruṣa*—is superior. As in the case of the word "past" (*atīta*).
The same criterion is applied to the "Abiding in Wisdom" chapter.
Regarding the phrase "recalling the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and the instructions of teachers and friends," this refers to the rest [of the categories].

The meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* assembly is that not only the understanding of the Tripiṭaka teachings is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); the instructions of teachers and the teachings of friends are likewise called wisdom derived from hearing.
Section: Regarding the statement that "the life of oxen and so forth is accomplished by grass," humans accomplish their lives through food, while oxen accomplish their lives through grass;
thus, life is what is accomplished.
Section. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the basis, etc.," the words and so forth are themselves the basis. Section.
As for the statement, "Although that [text] also speaks of it, it does not reach the point of being its text," this reconciles the contradiction.

That is to say, the meaning elucidated by the *sūtra* is not the thought itself; because the *sūtra* is the expressive teaching-text, it is said that it is "not its text. Therefore, there is also no [contradiction].
[This] contradicts the chapter. Regarding the passage from "within the Buddha-body" to "all are realized and understood," this text constitutes the second meaning.
Within it, the intent of the objection can be understood through reflection.

Section: As for the statement that the remaining [perfections] are combined because their meritorious characteristics are inferior, this is based on dividing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) into two categories. The merit of the other five perfections—[generosity, morality, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration]—is absent in those stages;

thus, they do not exist in the form realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Furthermore, the "analytical portion" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is absent there, as the analytical portion pertains to the preparatory stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prayoga*).

[The practitioner] proceeds. Because the formless [attainments] are inferior in wisdom, they cannot serve as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the superior Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Question:

It is accepted that the first untainted faculty (*anāsravendriya*) exists during both the stages of the Requisite Accumulation (*sambhāra*) and the Preparatory Stage (*prayoga*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle 7, states: "Because it is obtained through incidental cultivation (*pārśvabhāvanā*) alongside the superior Path of Seeing."
It is granted that the formless realm possesses the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). How then can there be no preparatory stages (*prayoga*) in the formless realm? The answer is:

the scope of the three faculties is broad, whereas the preparatory stage is narrow. It is simply said that the formless realm may possess the three faculties; it does not mean that all [beings therein] must necessarily have them.
Those who possess the provisions for enlightenment have not yet known that realm; those whose minds are still in the stage of preparatory application have not yet known that realm.

Thus, it is not at all unreasonable that there is nothing further to be known. Furthermore, it is like the first fifteen moments of mind prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), during which there is something yet to be known, because it is still to be realized.

It is called "unknown" (anājñāta), yet it cannot be termed "preparatory application" (prayoga). Therefore, the faculty of the unknown (anājñātam-ājñendriya) is broad, while preparatory application is narrow.
Alternatively, even those in the formless realm can perform a small portion of that preparatory application; however, such preparatory means are not the actual state [of the faculty itself].
That state relies exclusively upon the form realm (rūpadhātu). Reflect on this.

Section. As for Maudgalyāyana reaching [the state] where it is not through the wisdom of hearing: although he takes the ear-faculty of the desire realm as an object-condition, this is merely the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā) and not solely the wisdom of hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā).
Section. Why is it that the absence of the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mati*) is mentioned in the middle [stages]? This objection applies only to the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "It is not admitted that the three upper [stages] lack the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*)," this objection may apply to the seven stages (*sapta-bhūmi*). The general intent of the objection is to ask:
for what reason is there no similarity to the preparatory stage in the middle stages? Why, then, is it not admitted for the three upper stages?

There is [a distinction]. Regarding the statement that "the mind of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is called 'emergence'": the intention of this master is to say that after emerging from an uncontaminated meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one gives rise to a contaminated absorption;
this is called "emerging from the uncontaminated absorption. When one is in a contaminated absorption and emerges from that contaminated absorption, the opposite should be understood to apply.

If an ordinary person enters the first dhyāna and gives rise to three other types of minds belonging to the remaining dhyānas, this is called "emerging from the first dhyāna. All other cases should be understood accordingly. For now, let us pose the question based on arising from a lower stage to a higher mind: if one has attained the first dhyāna and gives rise to a mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is this also called "emerging"?
